Dead-Direction Signatures: A Cheap Spectral Reading of Singular Complexity

Tejas Pradeep Shirodkar Affiliation: IIIT, Hyderabad Email: tejas.shirodkar@research.iiit.ac.in    P. J. Narayanan Affiliation: IIIT, Hyderabad Email: pjn@iiit.ac.in
Abstract

Singular learning theory characterises the complexity of a deep network through the geometry of its loss singularities. The local learning coefficient (LLC), the standard estimator of Watanabe’s real log canonical threshold (RLCT, λ\lambda), reads this geometry as an integrated Bayesian scalar through SGLD, which needs per-task calibration and 10410^{4}-10610^{6} forward-backward passes per checkpoint. We introduce Dead-Direction Signatures (DDS), a family of cheap closed-form spectral readings of singular structure: each reads a network’s activation matrix or per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram at a chosen layer, replacing the SGLD posterior chain with spectral linear algebra. The readings rest on a dead-direction framework that predicts a structural correlation between activation- and Fisher-side spectra at any singular minimum, and a rank-multiplicative volume identity that single-eigenvalue monitors cannot produce: the active-volume logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) slope counts the dead directions, tracking the rank-deficit rr across r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\} (slope ratios 2.0,3.1,4.02.0,3.1,4.0 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 against the predicted 2,3,42,3,4), where the smallest eigenvalue is rank-blind. On reduced-rank regression with closed-form λ\lambda, calibrated LLC recovers λ\lambda at 99%99\% mean and the DDS observables rank-track it at the framework-predicted sign; on a non-linear modular-addition transformer DDS separates dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} across eighteen orders of magnitude where calibrated LLC at the protocol budget is rank-flat. Complementary to LLC’s integrated posterior reading, DDS gives a directional, layer-local handle on a network’s dead directions, read in closed form from its activation and gradient spectra.

1 Introduction

Singular learning theory locates the complexity of a deep network in the local geometry of its loss-singular set: the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) is the leading invariant, and it has been argued to be the right complexity measure on overparameterised models (Watanabe 2009; Watanabe 2018). In the empirical literature, the local learning coefficient (Lau et al. 2025, LLC;) has emerged as the canonical estimator of Watanabe’s RLCT in practice, the established choice for cross-model complexity ranking, posterior-Bayesian readings of singular structure, and developmental-stage detection during training (§2.1). It is also expensive: LLC requires 10410^{4}–10610^{6} forward–backward passes per checkpoint via SGLD sampling, an offline budget at LLM scale and a substantial cost even on parametric singular models.

We give a complementary readout. The framework of Shirodkar 2026 derives a directional Fisher decay rate at any singular minimum: along a dead direction of KL order kk, the directional Fisher decays as Θ⁡(t2​(k−1))\Theta(t^{2(k-1)}) along the parametric approach. The selection rule (Theorem 3) makes the bridge to Watanabe’s RLCT (denoted λ\lambda) explicit: the rate exponent 2​(k−1)2(k-1) recovers the directional RLCT contribution 1/(2​k)1/(2k) on smooth singular fibres, in original parameter coordinates, without resolution of singularities. From this primitive a cluster of cheap spectral observables follows, drawn from two natural matrices at each layer ℓ\ell: the activation matrix Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} (rows are per-sample post-activation hidden states, NN samples by hidden width hh), and the per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram Gℓ∈ℝh×hG_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times h} (the empirical covariance of layer-ℓ\ell gradients). The DDS observables are, by framework role: the rate observable λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) (smallest positive Fisher-Gram eigenvalue, predicted by the Fisher decay theorem); the volume observable logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) (active-spectrum log-volume, the curvature–volume class); and the activation-side dual σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) (the A–G dual of the rate observable, with layer-dependent sign). All three are framework-derived: the framework predicts a sign and an order of vanishing for each at any singular minimum. We collect these as Dead-Direction Signatures (DDS): a forward-pass-cheap reading of singular structure off a network’s activations and Fisher-Gram matrices in closed form. The four framework results we invoke (Fisher decay, selection rule + RLCT recovery, multi-layer KFAC bridge with A–G duality, curvature–volume rate chain) are restated with compact proof sketches in App. B.2, so the empirical claims below can be checked against an explicit derivation without opening the theory paper.

Three tests put pressure on different parts of the DDS claim; the contributions below carry the headline numbers and §4 the full protocols. The throughline separates the discriminating tests, the detection and rank-deficit counting that single-eigenvalue monitors cannot run, from the cross-cell rank-tracking against closed-form RLCT that turns out to be a sanity gate a naive capacity proxy also clears; a static structural correlation then adds a cross-testbed robustness reading, and an off-the-anchor probe carries DDS to one non-linear transformer where the structural sign survives but the trajectory rate breaks.

DDS trades LLC’s posterior chain for closed-form spectral reads. Calibrated LLC needs per-task SGLD calibration and a posterior chain per checkpoint (4,4004{,}400 forward–backward passes at our operating budget; the literature recommends 10410^{4}–10610^{6}). The activation-side σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) is one forward pass and an SVD, the cheap real-time read; the Fisher-side λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) and logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) assemble the per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram and take an O⁡(h3)O(h^{3}) eigendecomposition, orders of magnitude below an LLC chain on the parametric testbeds but the costliest DDS read as width climbs. The structural correlation closes that gap at scale, recovering the Fisher-side ordering from σmin2\sigma_{\min}^{2} at activation-side cost (§4).

Contributions.
  1. 1.

    Detection and rank-deficit counting, the framework’s discriminating tests. At a layer carrying a dead direction the smallest positive Fisher-Gram eigenvalue λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) collapses by orders of magnitude (∼246×\sim\!246\times at the bottleneck on the closed-form anchor, while the dimension-fixed boundary layer stays flat), detecting and localising it from a single backward pass. The active Fisher-volume logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) then counts the dead directions: its slope scales linearly in the rank-deficit rr while λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) is rr-invariant (Prop. 8 multi-direction generalisation). Across 77 noisy-bridge configurations (L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\}, D∈{20,50}D\in\{20,50\}, full and mini-batch SGD, 55 seeds, r=1..4r{=}1..4) the logdet+\log\det^{+} slope ratio tracks the rank-deficit (cell-wise means 2.0,3.1,4.02.0,3.1,4.0 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 against the predicted 2,3,42,3,4), a strict prefactor-free identity invisible to single-rank spectral monitors (§4.2, §4.1).

  2. 2.

    Closed-form RLCT ground truth, with the cross-cell rank-correlation as a sanity gate. On the Aoyagi 2005 anchor (analytical λ\lambda over [9,25][9,25]), a target-λ\lambda-calibrated LLC recovers λ\lambda at 99%99\% mean and DDS rate-chain observables rank-track λ\lambda at |ρ|∈[0.95,0.98]|\rho|\in[0.95,0.98] with the predicted sign; but calibrated LLC (+0.98+0.98) and a naive H⋅rH{\cdot}r capacity proxy (+0.99+0.99) clear the same bar, so the cross-cell correlation is a sanity gate, not a discriminator. On the 2424-cell Aoyagi 2024 deep-linear sweep λ\lambda is constant above saturation (200=d2/2200=d^{2}/2); DDS observables track that constancy while locked-config LLC reads the drifting local-LLC at w⋆w^{\star}, distinct from the global RLCT (Lau et al. 2025) (§4.1, App. B.6).

  3. 3.

    Off-the-anchor extension and a cross-testbed robustness reading. On a Nanda modular-addition width sweep at AdamW++CE (101101 of 120120 grokked cells, 44 widths × 30\times\,30 seeds) DDS observables span 55–1515 orders of magnitude and stay sign-coherent at |ρ|∈[0.62,0.96]|\rho|\in[0.62,0.96] vs dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}, where calibrated LLC at the protocol budget is rank-flat and a 9×9\times SGLD budget leaves it flat. The static structural correlation λmin+​(Gℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ)2\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2} holds at ρ≥+0.83\rho\geq+0.83 on canonical-aligned testbeds (Barak post-grok SGD++MSE; Nanda SGD++MSE no-grok), ρ=+1.000\rho{=}{+}1.000 on the analytic L=2L{=}2 bridge, and ρ=+0.75\rho{=}{+}0.75 at the AdamW++CE boundary (true-MC Fisher), where the trajectory-rate prediction fails but the static sign survives. The transformer probe here is single-architecture / single-task, with broader transformer coverage left as open empirical work (§4.3, §4.4, App. C).

Scope.

DDS is validated on parametric singular models with closed-form RLCT and one non-linear transformer width sweep. The directional Fisher-decay theorem and the selection rule are imported from the theory paper as cited prior results; calibrated LLC remains the canonical estimator for the posterior-Bayesian readings (singular fluctuations, WAIC, developmental-stage plateaus) that DDS does not provide.

2 Background and notation

For an analytic statistical family {pθ}\{p_{\theta}\} with Fisher information F⁡(θ)F(\theta) and pθ0=p∗p_{\theta_{0}}=p^{*}, the singular set Σ={θ:detF⁡(θ)=0}\Sigma=\{\theta:\det F(\theta)=0\} is where FF loses rank. Singular learning theory (Watanabe 2009) shows minima of K(θ):=KL(p∗∥pθ)K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(p^{*}\|p_{\theta}) in singular models lie on Σ\Sigma, and that KK vanishes along a unit direction uu at θ0\theta_{0} at a rate controlled by an integer KL order k≥1k\geq 1: K⁡(θ0+t​u)=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta_{0}+tu)=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}). Reading kk: k=1k{=}1 is an ordinary quadratic minimum (Fisher full rank along uu, the regular case); k=2k{=}2 is a quartic-flat dead direction along which FF vanishes as Θ⁡(t2)\Theta(t^{2}); larger kk means flatter, more degenerate. The rate exponent 2​(k−1)2(k-1) thus controls how fast FF collapses as the parameter approaches the singular minimum along uu. The RLCT λ\lambda decomposes into a directional 1/(2​k)1/(2k) contribution from the transversal dead direction plus a tangential term; the selection rule (Thm. 3) recovers that 1/(2​k)1/(2k) piece from our rate exponent 2​(k−1)2(k-1) in original coordinates, with the full normal-form derivation in App. B.2.

For a layer with weights WℓW_{\ell}, the KFAC factorisation (Martens and Grosse 2015) gives Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell} with Aℓ:=𝔼⁡[Xℓ−1​Xℓ−1⊤]A_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[X_{\ell-1}X_{\ell-1}^{\top}] and Gℓ:=𝔼⁡[δℓ​δℓ⊤]G_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}]; thus λmin​(Fℓ)=λmin​(Aℓ)​λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(F_{\ell})=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})\,\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}). We use Aℓ,GℓA_{\ell},G_{\ell} as canonical names. Other recurring symbols: LL depth, ℓ\ell layer index, hh hidden width; Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} activation matrix; uu dead direction (Def. 1).

2.1 Related work

Singular learning theory and LLC.

Watanabe’s singular learning theory (Watanabe 2009; Watanabe 2018) locates the complexity of an overparameterised model in the local geometry of its loss-singular set, with the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) as the leading invariant. The local learning coefficient (Lau et al. 2025, LLC;) is the canonical empirical estimator: SGLD sampling on the posterior near a singular minimum recovers Watanabe’s RLCT in practice. LLC has been extended to track developmental phase transitions during training (Hoogland et al. 2024) and to decompose into per-component restricted-LLC (Wang et al. 2025). We position DDS as a complementary readout on the same singular structure: where LLC integrates over the local posterior to return a Bayesian-WBIC-anchored quantity, DDS reads the spectra of the activations and Fisher-Gram in closed form at a single checkpoint. The two approaches answer different questions about the same singular geometry, and the cost ordering (the activation-side σmin\sigma_{\min} orders of magnitude below calibrated LLC per checkpoint on the testbeds here) lets DDS run at scales and cadences SGLD cannot match.

Closed-form RLCT lineage.

Aoyagi and Watanabe’s closed-form RLCT formulas for reduced-rank regression (Aoyagi and Watanabe 2005) and the recent extension to deep-linear nets (Aoyagi 2024) provide ground-truth λ\lambda values on parametric singular families, enabling validation against analytical RLCT rather than another estimator. The selection rule of Shirodkar 2026 (Thm. 3) is the formal bridge from our directional Fisher exponent to Watanabe’s RLCT: the rate 2​(k−1)2(k-1) recovers the directional contribution 1/(2​k)1/(2k) on smooth singular fibres in original parameter coordinates without resolution of singularities. Our use of Aoyagi-style closed-form RLCT testbeds in §4.1 is the empirical anchor for this bridge.

Spectral monitoring on activations and weights.

A parallel line summarises activation- or Fisher-side spectra as generalisation-correlated signatures: participation ratio on FFN activation covariances (Jha and Reagen 2026), streaming spectral entropy and top spectral gap on windowed activations (Ettori et al. 2025), the normalised Shannon entropy of Khanh et al. 2026, and the parameter-update top consecutive-singular-value ratio of Xu 2026. Marchenko–Pastur deviations on pretrained weights (Staats et al. 2024) and rank-collapse on pure-attention chains (Dong et al. 2021; Noci et al. 2022) read the same spectra at still other points; Boix-Adsera et al. 2023 report training-trajectory rank evolution, a different object from the singular-minimum rank deficit DDS targets. DDS reads the Fisher-Gram bottom directly through the rate-chain observables (λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G)) and the activation-side dual σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}), with framework-derived sign and per-layer prescription tied to the directional RLCT contribution 1/(2​k)1/(2k) via the Fisher decay theorem and A–G duality (Theorem 2, full proof App. A). The prior signatures correlate spectra with generalisation, and we report them as complementary observation points without a quantitative head-to-head. Random-matrix characterisations of the Fisher / Hessian spectrum at large width (Pennington and Worah 2018; Karakida et al. 2019; Karakida et al. 2021) address the bulk at random init under mean-field or Gaussian-entry assumptions; the DDS observables read the trained-checkpoint bottom spectrum at a chosen layer, used both as static per-checkpoint structural identities and as directional rates along the singular-minimum approach. We use random-matrix arguments defensively for the n/dn/d calibration of the measurement protocol.

Algebraic dead directions in LayerNorm.

An instantiation of the same dead-direction framework gives the cheapest read of the primitive: for LayerNorm models the dead direction is fixed algebraically by the normalization affine, v⋆=γ−1/‖γ−1‖v^{\star}=\gamma^{-1}/\|\gamma^{-1}\|, recoverable from the layer parameter with no forward pass (Shirodkar and Narayanan 2026). That algebraic read is exact for LayerNorm models. DDS’s spectral observables (σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}), the Fisher-Gram spectrum) are architecture-general and read the same primitive at a forward-pass or Fisher cost, two points on a cost–generality spectrum for the same dead-direction object.

KFAC and the Fisher estimand.

Our measurement protocol uses the KFAC factorisation (Martens and Grosse 2015; Grosse and Martens 2016; Eschenhagen et al. 2023) with the Fisher estimand matched to the task: the empirical (true-label) Fisher on the MSE testbeds, where it coincides with the model Fisher at the minimum, and the true-MC (model-sampled) Fisher on the cross-entropy testbed, where the empirical Fisher is an unreliable proxy (Kunstner et al. 2019) that collapses at zero loss. George et al. 2018 introduced the eigenbasis variant. The KFAC factorisation’s analytical use (the A–G duality, Cor. 25) is established in Shirodkar 2026; we use it as a measurement primitive only.

3 The structural correlation

At any singular minimum the activation-side and Fisher-side bottoms of the spectrum vanish together at a predictable ratio. The coupling is the single structural prediction DDS rests on, stated below. The supporting framework (Fisher decay theorem, selection rule, multi-layer KFAC bridge, A–G duality) lives in the theory paper and is used here as a cited prior.

Definition 1 (Dead direction).

A unit direction u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a dead direction at θ0\theta_{0} if u⊤​F​(θ⁡(t))​u→0u^{\top}F(\theta(t))u\to 0 as t→0t\to 0 along θ⁡(t):=θ0+t​u\theta(t):=\theta_{0}+tu. The KL order along uu is the integer k≥1k\geq 1 with K⁡(θ⁡(t))=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta(t))=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}), c>0c>0. (Unrelated to the activation-level “dead ReLU” phenomenon despite the lexical overlap.)

Theorem 2 (Structural correlation between Fisher and activation spectra).

At any singular minimum of an LL-layer network with KFAC-decomposable Fisher information Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell}, along a canonical-aligned approach θ⁡(t)\theta(t) to the minimum:

λmin+​(Gℓ​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)),σmin​(Xℓ​(θ⁡(t)))2/N=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ),\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}(\theta(t)))\;=\;\Theta(t^{2(L-\ell)}),\qquad\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}(\theta(t)))^{2}/N\;=\;\Theta(t^{2\ell}),

at every layer ℓ\ell. Both quantities vanish as t→0t\to 0 as positive powers of tt, so they are co-monotonic along the approach and the Spearman rank correlation between them tends to +1+1 in the asymptotic regime.

Sketch.

By the multi-layer KFAC bridge (Theorem 21 of the theory paper), the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Fisher-Gram at layer ℓ\ell satisfies λmin+​(Gℓ​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ))\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}(\theta(t)))=\Theta(t^{2(L-\ell)}) along a canonical-aligned approach. By the A–G duality corollary (Cor. 25), the activation-side dual is λmin​(Aℓ+1​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ)\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell+1}(\theta(t)))=\Theta(t^{2\ell}), and σmin​(Xℓ)2/N→λmin​(Aℓ+1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2}/N\to\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell+1}) almost surely by the strong law (the rows of XℓX_{\ell} are iid under the Gaussian-isotropic input assumption of Theorem 2). Both Fisher and activation bottoms are positive powers of tt with strictly positive exponents; rank correlation between any two such monotone trajectories tends to +1+1 in the asymptotic limit. Full proof in App. A. ∎

The three DDS observables (smallest activation singular value σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}), smallest positive Fisher-Gram eigenvalue λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}), log-volume logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell})) read this coupled geometry from the activation or the gradient side. §4 validates the correlation across regime cells, with a deterministic limit on the analytic L=2L{=}2 bridge and a boundary check on AdamW++CE where canonical alignment is violated.

4 Experiments

DDS detects a dead direction and counts how many directions are dead, two reads a single-eigenvalue monitor cannot give. §4.1 pins detection and rank-tracking to closed-form RLCT ground truth, where the cross-cell rank-correlation turns out to be a sanity gate that even a naive capacity proxy clears. §4.2 is the discriminating quantitative test, the counting identity. §4.3 carries the observables off the anchor to a non-linear transformer at AdamW++CE, and §4.4 reports the static structural correlation as a robustness reading. Tab. 1 summarises the per-testbed Spearman ρ\rho; per-claim assumptions and validation loci are in App. B.1.

4.1 Closed-form RLCT anchor (Aoyagi reduced-rank regression)

If DDS tracks Watanabe’s RLCT, the first thing to demand is agreement with the analytical λ\lambda where ground truth is closed-form. Reduced-rank regression (RRR) is the canonical singular family with closed-form RLCT: it factors a teacher matrix M⋆∈ℝN×MM^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M} of rank rr through a hidden bottleneck of width HH, so the trained model is W2​W1W_{2}W_{1} with W1∈ℝH×MW_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times M}, W2∈ℝN×HW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H}. The Aoyagi–Watanabe closed form (Aoyagi and Watanabe 2005) gives the RLCT λ\lambda as a function of (M,N,H,r)(M,N,H,r) alone (input dim MM, output dim NN, bottleneck HH, truth rank rr), providing analytical ground truth against which any RLCT estimator can be calibrated. Our Aoyagi 2005 anchor fixes M=10,N=5M{=}10,N{=}5 and sweeps H∈{2,3,4,5}H\in\{2,3,4,5\} and r∈{1,…,min⁡(N,H)}r\in\{1,\ldots,\min(N,H)\}, giving 1414 realisable cells (truth rank ≤\leq model capacity) at λ∈[9,25]\lambda\in[9,25]. The Aoyagi 2024 deep-linear net (DLN) sweep (Aoyagi 2024) extends this to a 33-matrix product W3​W2​W1W_{3}W_{2}W_{1} with shared input/output dim d=20d{=}20 and hidden width h∈{16,20,24,32,64,128}h\in\{16,20,24,32,64,128\}; the truth rank is 20−rd20-\mathrm{rd} where the rank deficit rd∈{1,2,3,4}\mathrm{rd}\in\{1,2,3,4\} counts how many directions the truth is degenerate in. The saturation threshold is h≥rank⁡(M⋆)h\geq\mathrm{rank}(M^{\star}): at and above it the model has enough capacity to express the truth and the closed-form RLCT becomes provably independent of hh, fixed by the truth’s rank alone. With d=20d{=}20, the h∈{20,24,32,64,128}h\in\{20,24,32,64,128\} cells sit at or above saturation across all rd\mathrm{rd}; the h=16h{=}16 cell sits below it for rd<4\mathrm{rd}<4. The constancy-in-hh comparison below uses the above-saturation cells, where the analytical RLCT is constant by design; the unrealisable h=16,rd<4h{=}16,\mathrm{rd}<4 subset is excluded from the constancy claim. Calibrated LLC is retrofitted on every cell with a locked SGLD config (per-testbed 5×55\times 5 grid + 9×9\times saturation gate); see App. B.6 for the lock procedure.

Detection comes first. At the bottleneck layer the smallest positive Fisher-Gram eigenvalue λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) collapses ∼246×\sim\!246\times the instant a dead direction is present, while the dimension-fixed boundary layer stays flat to 0.3%0.3\% (Fig. 2); the collapse is one backward pass, and it localises the dead direction to the bottleneck. The magnitudes are trustworthy against the closed form: under a target-λ\lambda SGLD calibration, calibrated LLC recovers the analytical λ\lambda at 99%99\% mean across the 1414 cells (App. B.5). Cross-cell rank-tracking is a sanity gate. The rate-chain observables λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) and logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) rank-track λ\lambda at |ρ|∈[0.95,0.98]|\rho|\in[0.95,0.98] on the dimension-fixed boundary layer with the framework-predicted sign, and σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) reads the truth-rank at ρ=+0.89\rho=+0.89; but calibrated LLC (+0.98+0.98) and a naive H⋅rH{\cdot}r capacity proxy (+0.99+0.99) clear the same bar (Fig. 3), so the cross-cell correlation is a passing bar every complexity-monotone observable meets, not a discriminator (the rankings hold across a 4×4\times σ\sigma-noise range, App. B.6). On the Aoyagi 2024 DLN sweep, λ\lambda is constant in hh above saturation and DDS observables track that constancy, while calibrated LLC at the locked-config budget reads the local-LLC at the trained w⋆w^{\star}, which Lau et al. 2025 distinguish from the global RLCT.

4.2 Rank-multiplicative volume identity (discriminating test)

Sign and rank-correlation tests are a passing bar; the discriminating test is a quantitative identity any monotone observable would fail. The framework provides one: at a singular minimum with rank-deficit rr, logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope scales linearly in rr while λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope is rr-invariant (Prop. 8 multi-direction generalisation). The slope at rank-deficit rr is rr times the rank-11 slope, with no free prefactor. Single-eigenvalue spectral monitors are rank-blind to this identity by construction.

We measure across 77 noisy-bridge configurations (L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\}, D∈{20,50}D\in\{20,50\}, full and mini-batch SGD, σ=0.1\sigma{=}0.1, 55 seeds each), running each trajectory at rank-deficit r=1,…,4r{=}1,\dots,4 (M⋆=diag⁡(1,…,1,0,…)M^{\star}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots) with the last rr entries zero). Cells use depth-controlled init t0​(L)=(1/16)1/Lt_{0}(L)=(1/16)^{1/L} to hold the initial dead-direction product t0L=1/16t_{0}^{L}=1/16 constant across LL, isolating the rate prediction from the asymptotic-regime accessibility (Rem. 11). The logdet+\log\det^{+} slope ratio tracks the rank-deficit across all four ranks (Fig. 4): cell-wise means 2.0,3.1,4.02.0,3.1,4.0 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 against the predicted 2,3,42,3,4, the r=2r{=}2 ratio inside the ±10%\pm 10\% falsification band, while the matching λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+} slopes stay rr-invariant (rate-chain ρ=0.985\rho{=}0.985). Per-cell and per-layer breakdowns are in App. B.8.2.

4.3 Off-the-anchor extension on a non-linear transformer

The closed-form anchor pins DDS to ground truth in the canonical-aligned regime; the natural next question is what survives off it. We run the same observables on a non-linear architecture trained with AdamW++CE, where the canonical-alignment hypothesis is violated. This is the cleanest single-axis stress test. We use the Nanda modular-addition setup (Nanda et al. 2023) at dmodel∈{32,64,128,256}d_{\mathrm{model}}\in\{32,64,128,256\} (3030 seeds per width, 101101 of 120120 grokked) under AdamW++CE, with per-width SGLD calibration locked via a 5×55\times 5 grid plus 9×9\times saturation gate. The framework predicts (Theorems 2, 9, 25): wider model →\to more degenerate Fisher →\to smaller λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), more negative logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G), smaller σmin\sigma_{\min}. Every DDS observable spans 55–1515 orders of magnitude across the four widths, remains monotone in dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}, and is sign-coherent at |ρ|∈[0.62,0.96]|\rho|\in[0.62,0.96], with logdet+(Gh2)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) at the high end (|ρ|=0.965|\rho|{=}0.965, 35%35\% rel-std). Calibrated LLC at the protocol 4,4004{,}400-step budget is rank-flat on the same sweep (ρ=−0.07\rho{=}{-}0.07), and a 9×9\times-budget re-run does not lift it (App. B.6). The dynamic range and sign-coherence are what the 44-distinct-widths setup can test; the cross-cell Spearman has heavy tied-rank dependence, and this is one architecture on one task. Broadening the rate and structural-correlation reads (attention-only chains, deeper transformers, more widths, other algorithmic tasks) is open empirical work.

4.4 Static structural correlation (robustness reading)

The static structural identity λmin+​(Gℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ)2\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2} couples the Fisher-side and activation-side spectra at any singular minimum (Theorem 21, Cor. 25; full proof in App. A). It supplies the same Fisher-side ordering as λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) at activation-side cost, which matters at LLM widths where the Fisher-side full-spectrum is expensive (cost ordering below). The discriminating quantitative test lives on the volume side (§4.2); here we report the static identity as a robustness reading across testbeds. Two canonical-aligned non-trivial testbeds. ρ=+0.832±0.126\rho=+0.832\pm 0.126 on Barak sparse parity (Barak et al. 2022) SGD++MSE Phase A (3030 seeds; post-grok descent into the singular minimum), and ρ=+0.846±0.014\rho=+0.846\pm 0.014 on the Nanda 11-block transformer SGD++MSE no-grok cell (1010 seeds). Deterministic check. On the analytic L=2L{=}2 canonical bridge (linear, deterministic GF, MSE; 1010 seeds), ρ=+1.000\rho=+1.000, the analytical limit where ρ\rho reduces to algebra. The theorem predicts ρ→+1\rho\to+1 in the strict asymptotic limit; finite-tt deviations and finite-NN Marchenko–Pastur noise on A^ℓ+1\widehat{A}_{\ell+1} shrink the observed correlation, and the ordering matches: deterministic at the limit, Barak loosened by finite N/D≈2N/D\approx 2 and the 3030-seed dispersion. Boundary-of-applicability check. Nanda 11-block transformer AdamW++CE (groks; 1010 seeds, true-MC Fisher) gives ρ=+0.751±0.106\rho=+0.751\pm 0.106. On AdamW++CE the canonical-alignment hypothesis is violated (Adam’s diagonal preconditioner is non-equivariant under CE’s logit-shift symmetry; Rem. 80), so the trajectory-level prediction does not strictly apply; the residual coupling rests on the KFAC factorisation Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell} at the singular minimum itself, independent of the optimiser. Slope-2 prediction. On Barak Phase A, 44 of 55 seeds give trajectory-rate slope x¯=2.06±0.20\bar{x}=2.06\pm 0.20 (R2∈[0.87,0.97]R^{2}\in[0.87,0.97]), agreeing with the noisy-bridge sweep (§4.2); higher n/Dn/D compresses the geometric event below save-cadence resolution (App. B.8).

Cost ordering.

The four observables sit at different training-loop cadences. σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) is one forward pass plus an SVD (O⁡(N​h2)O(Nh^{2})) and runs at real-time cadence at any width we tested. u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu at a known direction is one FBP (O⁡(h)O(h)), checkpoint cadence. The Fisher-side full-spectrum observables λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) and logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) assemble the per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram and take its O⁡(h3)O(h^{3}) eigendecomposition, periodic cadence on small models and offline at LLM width. Calibrated LLC’s 4,4004{,}400-FBP SGLD chain is offline at any scale we tested. On a Barak post-grok checkpoint (h=500h{=}500), in wall-clock, the Fisher-side observables are ∼300×\sim\!300\times cheaper than calibrated LLC and σmin\sigma_{\min} is ∼130×\sim\!130\times cheaper (App. B.8.1). At LLM widths the ordering shifts: σmin\sigma_{\min} and u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu scale roughly linearly in hh and stay cheap, while the Fisher-side eigendecomposition scales as O⁡(h3)O(h^{3}) and becomes the costliest DDS read. The structural correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin2)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min}^{2}) (§4.4) recovers the Fisher-side ordering through σmin\sigma_{\min} at activation-side cost; per-cadence recipes and per-width wall-clock numbers are in App. B.4.

5 Discussion

What we showed.

DDS detects and counts dead directions through cheap closed-form spectral reads of a network’s activations and Fisher-Gram, complementary to calibrated LLC; the per-checkpoint cost ordering and how it shifts with width are in §4.

The three DDS observables read singular structure from complementary sides of the same per-layer object. σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) reads activation rank-deficiency, λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) reads gradient-Gram rank-deficiency, and logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) reads the active gradient-Gram log-volume. The framework’s structural correlation states that activation and gradient rank-deficiency reflect the same singular geometry coupled through the KFAC factorisation, which anchors the three observables to one another. The volume-side rank-multiplicative identity is the quantitative structural prediction this anchoring produces; it cannot be reduced to sign or rank correlation, and §4 bears this out as the discriminating test where the cross-cell rank-tracking is only a sanity gate.

Alternative explanations considered.

(i) Calibrated-LLC width-flatness / drift is a budget artefact. Ruled out by a 9×9\times-larger SGLD budget at d=128d{=}128 on the Nanda sweep: within-cell SGLD std falls 1.50×1.50\times but across-seed std falls only 1.05×1.05\times, so per-seed initialisation variance dominates SGLD measurement variance at this calibration cell, and the drift on the DLN sweep is consistent with the App. I local-vs-global RLCT distinction (Lau et al. 2025) (App. B.6). (ii) Transformer cross-architecture extension is contingent on grokking. The sign-coherent |ρ|∈[0.62,0.96]|\rho|\in[0.62,0.96] reading is on the 101101 grokked cells; whether DDS extends to non-grokked transformers remains open.

Where DDS applies and where it doesn’t.

(a) Static observables apply at any singular minimum, conditional on one being present. The three DDS readings are algebraic identities of the per-layer geometry; they are testbed-broad across every optimiser, loss, and architecture we tested. They go quiet on data without rank-deficient teachers or training that does not reach a singular minimum: there is nothing dead to read. The geometry is a property of the problem the network is solving. (b) Trajectory rate-fits additionally require an actual descent. The rank-multiplicative identity and the per-layer rate ladder need canonical alignment, a theorem-compatible preconditioner (SGD on GG-invariant metrics), and the trajectory entering the asymptotic regime where t→0t\to 0. The third precondition is data-and-training-dependent: a network that never settles into the singular minimum (training stopped short, regularisation absent, optimiser parked in a non-singular basin) leaves the rate undefined. (c) Architectural reach tested. The rank-multi identity is validated on 77 noisy-bridge configurations; the transformer cross-architecture probe is one task on a single-block transformer with 44 widths. Width sweeps on attention-only chains, deeper transformers, and other small-algorithmic tasks are open empirical work. (d) Posterior-Bayesian summaries. The local-posterior summaries (Watanabe’s multiplicity mm, the singular fluctuation ν\nu, posterior-WAIC, and the developmental-stage trajectory plateaus (Hoogland et al. 2024)) integrate over the posterior and read a complementary slice of the same singular structure. (e) Methodological caveats. The dimension-fixed boundary layer prescription (App. B.6) was identified on the Aoyagi anchor and applied across the DLN sweep, the Nanda extension, and the structural-correlation testbeds; on architectures with no obvious bottleneck the rule must be tested before being trusted.

Falsifiers.

Three checks would force revision. (F1) An Aoyagi-anchor cell where rate-chain observables carry the wrong sign against λ\lambda; we find none across the 1414 cells where λ\lambda varies. (F2) A canonical-aligned noisy-bridge cell at L≥4L\geq 4 where the logdet+\log\det^{+} slope ratio at rank-deficit rr deviates from rr by more than ±10%\pm 10\%; across r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\} the 77 configurations read 1.96,3.13,3.971.96,3.13,3.97 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 against the predicted 2,3,42,3,4. (F3) A canonical-aligned-regime architecture where ρ⁡(λmin+​(Gℓ),σmin​(Xℓ)2)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}),\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2}) across checkpoints reads ≤0\leq 0.

Outlook.

DDS gives the first directional, parameter-local handle on singular complexity. Three follow-ons sit close: rank-collapse pretraining monitors, LoRA placement along measured dead directions, and complexity ranking on architectures where SGLD calibration is impractical; further out, the same dead-direction reads should extend from λ\lambda to the rest of the Watanabe triple (mm, ν\nu) and WAIC without SGLD. Complementing LLC’s posterior readouts, singular complexity, until now an offline Bayesian invariant, gets a cheaper diagnostic that travels with the network it describes.

Appendix A Theoretical foundations: proof of the structural correlation

We restate Theorem 2 of Section 3 and give a complete proof, citing the bridge framework as a black-box prior result. The framework’s foundations (Fisher decay theorem, multi-layer KFAC bridge, A–G duality) are derived in the theory paper. The present paper validates the structural correlation empirically across four testbeds and contributes the theorem-to-empirics assembly given here.

Setup.

Fix an LL-layer network with KFAC-decomposable layer-ℓ\ell Fisher Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell}, where Aℓ:=𝔼⁡[Xℓ−1​Xℓ−1⊤]A_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[X_{\ell-1}X_{\ell-1}^{\top}] is the layer-ℓ\ell input covariance and Gℓ:=𝔼⁡[δℓ​δℓ⊤]G_{\ell}:=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}] is the layer-ℓ\ell pre-activation gradient covariance. Let θ0\theta_{0} be a singular minimum of the population KL K(θ):=KL(p⋆∥pθ)K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(p^{\star}\|p_{\theta}), and let θ⁡(t):=θ0+t​u\theta(t):=\theta_{0}+tu for uu a unit dead direction of KL order k≥1k\geq 1 (Definition 1). We assume the canonical-aligned approach hypothesis used in the multi-layer KFAC bridge (Theorem 21 of the theory paper): along the trajectory θ⁡(t)\theta(t), the per-layer dead-direction projector commutes with the KFAC factors in the limit t→0t\to 0. The theory paper derives this hypothesis as a generic consequence of balanced-init linear / smooth-nonlinear gradient flow on KK. The hypothesis is not generic on Adam-class trajectories (Remark 80); see the second remark below.

Theorem 3 (Structural correlation between Fisher and activation spectra; restated from Section 3).

Under the canonical-aligned approach hypothesis, at every layer ℓ∈{1,…,L−1}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}:

λmin+​(Gℓ​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)),σmin​(Xℓ​(θ⁡(t)))2/N=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ),t→0.\lambda^{+}_{\min}\!\left(G_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2(L-\ell)}\right),\qquad\sigma_{\min}\!\left(X_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)^{\!2}\!/N\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2\ell}\right),\qquad t\to 0.

Both quantities vanish as t→0t\to 0 as strictly positive powers of tt, so they are co-monotonic along the approach and

ρSpearman​(λmin+​(Gℓ),σmin​(Xℓ)2/N)→a.s.+1\rho_{\mathrm{Spearman}}\!\left(\lambda^{+}_{\min}(G_{\ell}),\;\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2}/N\right)\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;+1

in the asymptotic limit N→∞N\to\infty, min⁡ti→0\min t_{i}\to 0 over a sample {ti}i=1M\{t_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} along the approach.

Proof.

The proof proceeds in five steps. Steps 1 and 2 invoke the bridge framework as black-box prior results; Steps 3–5 are the theorem-to-empirics assembly.

Step 1 (Fisher-side rate; cited). The multi-layer KFAC bridge (Theorem 21 of the theory paper) gives, along the canonical-aligned approach,

λmin+​(Gℓ​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)),t→0,\lambda^{+}_{\min}\!\left(G_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2(L-\ell)}\right),\qquad t\to 0,

where λmin+\lambda^{+}_{\min} denotes the smallest non-zero eigenvalue. The exponent 2​(L−ℓ)2(L-\ell) counts the gradient-side path-length from layer ℓ\ell to the output through the dead direction uu.

Step 2 (Activation-side population rate; cited). The A–G duality corollary (Cor. 25 of the theory paper) gives, on the same approach,

λmin​(Aℓ+1​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ),\lambda_{\min}\!\left(A_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\right)\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2\ell}\right),

where the exponent 2​ℓ2\ell counts the activation-side path-length from the input to layer ℓ\ell through uu. The duality λmin​(Aℓ+1)⋅λmin+​(Gℓ)=Θ⁡(t2​L)\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell+1})\cdot\lambda^{+}_{\min}(G_{\ell})=\Theta(t^{2L}) is the structural identity behind the layer-symmetric rate decomposition.

Step 3 (Sample-to-population on the activation side). The bridge framework’s Gaussian-isotropic input model (Theorem 21 of the theory paper) makes the rows of Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} i.i.d. samples. Under this assumption, the empirical activation Gram is

A^ℓ+1​(θ⁡(t)):=Xℓ​(θ⁡(t))⊤​Xℓ​(θ⁡(t))/N,\widehat{A}_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\;:=\;X_{\ell}(\theta(t))^{\top}X_{\ell}(\theta(t))\,/\,N,

and the strong law of large numbers gives entrywise almost-sure convergence,

A^ℓ+1​(θ⁡(t))→a.s.Aℓ+1​(θ⁡(t))as ​N→∞\widehat{A}_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;A_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\quad\text{as }N\to\infty

at fixed tt. Weyl’s inequality |λi​(A^)−λi​(A)|≤‖A^−A‖op|\lambda_{i}(\widehat{A})-\lambda_{i}(A)|\leq\|\widehat{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}} lifts entrywise convergence to spectral convergence, so

σmin​(Xℓ​(θ⁡(t)))2/N=λmin​(A^ℓ+1​(θ⁡(t)))→a.s.λmin​(Aℓ+1​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ)\sigma_{\min}\!\left(X_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)^{\!2}\!/N\;=\;\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\widehat{A}_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\right)\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;\lambda_{\min}\!\left(A_{\ell+1}(\theta(t))\right)\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2\ell}\right)

combining Step 2 with the convergence above.

Step 4 (Co-monotonicity). Combining Steps 1 and 3, at every ℓ∈{1,…,L−1}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\} both quantities vanish as strictly positive powers of tt:

λmin+​(Gℓ​(θ⁡(t)))=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)),σmin​(Xℓ​(θ⁡(t)))2/N=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ).\lambda^{+}_{\min}\!\left(G_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2(L-\ell)}\right),\qquad\sigma_{\min}\!\left(X_{\ell}(\theta(t))\right)^{\!2}\!/N\;=\;\Theta\!\left(t^{2\ell}\right).

The exponents satisfy 2​(L−ℓ)≥22(L-\ell)\geq 2 and 2​ℓ≥22\ell\geq 2 for ℓ∈{1,…,L−1}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}, so both are strictly positive. Two strictly positive monotone-decreasing functions of tt produce identical rank orderings on any deterministic sample {ti}\{t_{i}\} with min⁡ti→0\min t_{i}\to 0, up to ties of measure zero.

Step 5 (Asymptotic Spearman). The Spearman rank correlation between two sequences is, by definition, the Pearson correlation of their rank transforms. Identical rank orderings yield Pearson correlation +1+1 on the rank-transformed sequences, hence Spearman correlation +1+1. The almost-sure convergence in Step 3 lifts the population-level identity to the sample level: as N→∞N\to\infty and min⁡ti→0\min t_{i}\to 0,

ρSpearman​(λmin+​(Gℓ),σmin​(Xℓ)2/N)→a.s.+1.∎\rho_{\mathrm{Spearman}}\!\left(\lambda^{+}_{\min}(G_{\ell}),\;\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2}/N\right)\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;+1.\qed
Remark (finite-tt, finite-NN behaviour).

The theorem’s ρ→+1\rho\to+1 is asymptotic. Two sources of finite-sample shrinkage matter at the testbeds in Section 4.4.

Finite tt: the rate expansions in Steps 1 and 2 carry subleading O⁡(t)O(t) corrections from second-order terms in the bridge framework (Theorem 21 of the theory paper). Off-asymptotic, two trajectories with different leading exponents but matching subleading terms can produce rank disagreements of order O⁡(t)O(t). This shrinks the observed correlation by O⁡(t)O(t) at finite distance from the singular minimum.

Finite NN: the SLLN convergence in Step 3 has rate ‖A^−A‖op=O⁡(D/N)\|\widehat{A}-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\sqrt{D/N}) on D×DD\times D Wishart-style Gram matrices (Marchenko–Pastur). When σmin​(A)=Θ⁡(t2​ℓ)\sigma_{\min}(A)=\Theta(t^{2\ell}) is small relative to the noise floor O⁡(D/N)O(\sqrt{D/N}), the empirical σmin​(A^)\sigma_{\min}(\widehat{A}) saturates at the noise floor and decouples from the population value. This is the regime where Barak’s N/D≈2N/D\approx 2 at the deepest checkpoints loosens the observed correlation; it is the same effect that motivates the n/Dn/D measurement-stability rule of the experiments appendix.

The four-testbed experiment (Section 4.4) measures the finite-tt, finite-NN correlation across regimes with different distance-to-asymptotic and different sample size; the predicted ordering (canonical bridge cleanest, Barak/Nanda noisier) is what we observe.

Remark (off-canonical regimes and Adam-class trajectories).

The theorem requires the canonical-aligned approach hypothesis. On Adam-class trajectories the hypothesis is generically violated: Adam’s diagonal preconditioner is non-equivariant under continuous loss symmetries (CE logit-shift, ReLU rescaling), and the per-layer dead-direction projector does not commute with the KFAC factors along the trajectory. Remark 80 of the theory paper establishes this via direct calculation; the empirical drift on the gauge mode is reported in the cited mod-add factorial.

The structural correlation does not require the canonical-alignment hypothesis to hold strictly along the trajectory. At the singular minimum itself, the KFAC factorisation Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell} holds independent of the optimiser that reached the minimum, and the rank deficiency is shared between the two factors regardless of the alignment of the trajectory. The Adam++CE row of the four-testbed experiment (ρ=+0.751±0.106\rho=+0.751\pm 0.106 at 1010 seeds, true-MC Fisher; Section 4.4) tests the geometric coupling under the off-canonical preconditioner. It is the lowest of the four testbeds, where the canonical-alignment hypothesis fails most cleanly, and the cross-seed mean stays well above zero. The geometric coupling survives the canonical-alignment violation and loosens.

Connection to the rate exponents in the body.

The theorem’s 2​(L−ℓ)2(L-\ell) and 2​ℓ2\ell exponents enter the empirical predictions of Section 4 in two ways. (i) The cross-cell sign predictions on the Aoyagi grids and the Nanda width sweep follow from the leading-rate signs: wider model →\to more degenerate Fisher →\to smaller λmin+​(G)\lambda^{+}_{\min}(G), more negative logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G), smaller σmin\sigma_{\min}. (ii) The trajectory-rate readout of u⊤​Gℓ​uu^{\top}G_{\ell}u along the canonical-aligned approach (App. B.8.2) inherits the per-layer ladder 2​(L−ℓ)2(L-\ell) as a direct corollary; the validation of that ladder on parametric autoencoders is at three-decimal precision in the theory paper, and on Barak SGD++MSE the rank-correlation reading is +0.832±0.126+0.832\pm 0.126 across 3030 seeds. The trajectory rate-readout is appendix-only in the present paper; the body relies only on the structural correlation proven above.

B.2 Key results from the framework, with proof sketches

The empirical claims rest on four results of Shirodkar 2026. We restate each in compact form with a 2–3 line proof sketch; full proofs (with all assumptions, supporting lemmas, and architectural extensions) live in the theory paper. Throughout, F⁡(θ)=𝔼x​[∇θ​log​pθ​(x)​∇θ​log​pθ​(x)⊤]F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(x)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(x)^{\top}] is the Fisher information; K(θ):=KL(p⋆∥pθ)K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(p^{\star}\|p_{\theta}); Σ={θ:detF=0}\Sigma=\{\theta:\det F=0\}. A direction uu at θ0∈Σ\theta_{0}\in\Sigma has KL order kk if K⁡(θ0+t​u)=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta_{0}+tu)=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}) with c>0c>0.

Setup recall: Fisher = expected Hessian of KK.

For a regular family F⁡(θ)=∇2K​(θ)|θ=θ0F(\theta)=\nabla^{2}K(\theta)\big|_{\theta=\theta_{0}} at the truth (and in the singular case the same identity holds in the directions where the second moment is finite). This is the bridge from the analytic order of KK to the rate of FF along uu.

T1. Directional Fisher decay (Theorem 2, theory paper).

Along a dead direction of KL order k≥1k\geq 1:

u⊤​F​(θ0+t​u)​u=Θ⁡(t2​(k−1))as ​t→0.u^{\top}F(\theta_{0}+tu)\,u\;=\;\Theta\!\big(t^{2(k-1)}\big)\quad\text{as }t\to 0.

Sketch. Differentiate K⁡(θ0+t​u)=c​t2​k+O⁡(t2​k+1)K(\theta_{0}+tu)=c\,t^{2k}+O(t^{2k+1}) twice in tt: K′′=2​k​(2​k−1)​c​t2​k−2+O⁡(t2​k−1)K^{\prime\prime}=2k(2k-1)c\,t^{2k-2}+O(t^{2k-1}). Identifying K′′=u⊤​∇2K​uK^{\prime\prime}=u^{\top}\nabla^{2}K\,u at the perturbed point and using Fisher == Hessian of KK in directions where the score has finite second moment gives the rate. The case k=1k=1 (regular minimum) recovers Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) as expected.

T2. Selection rule + RLCT recovery (Theorem 3, theory paper).

On a smooth singular fibre of dimension mm at θ0\theta_{0}, write the local KL in normal-crossing form K∼u2​k+v12+⋯+vm2K\sim u^{2k}+v_{1}^{2}+\cdots+v_{m}^{2} (transversal coordinate uu of order 2​k2k, mm tangential coordinates of order 22). Then the local RLCT contribution is

λ^=12​k+m2,with the directional contribution ​12​k​ matched by our exponent ​2​(k−1)​ via ​λ^dir=12​k.\hat{\lambda}\;=\;\frac{1}{2k}+\frac{m}{2}\,,\qquad\text{with the directional contribution }\tfrac{1}{2k}\text{ matched by our exponent }2(k-1)\text{ via }\hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{dir}}=\tfrac{1}{2k}.

Sketch. The volume of {θ:K⁡(θ)≤ε}\{\theta:K(\theta)\leq\varepsilon\} scales as ε1/(2​k)\varepsilon^{1/(2k)} in the transversal direction (one dimension at order 2​k2k) and ε1/2\varepsilon^{1/2} in each tangential direction (mm at order 22); summing exponents and applying the Hironaka resolution [Hironaka 1964] identifies λ^\hat{\lambda}. The transversal exponent 1/(2​k)1/(2k) is the directional invariant our rate theorem returns in original coordinates without resolution.

T3. Multi-layer KFAC bridge (Theorem 21, theory paper).

Under the symmetric canonical-aligned approach Wℓ​(t)=Wℓ⋆+t⋅δℓW_{\ell}(t)=W_{\ell}^{\star}+t\cdot\delta_{\ell} on an LL-layer feedforward (or pre-norm residual) network, with δℓ\delta_{\ell} aligned to the dead direction:

σmin​(Xℓ​(t))=N⋅Θ⁡(tℓ),uℓ⊤​Gℓ​(t)​uℓ=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)),λmin+​(Gℓ)=Θ⁡(t2​(L−ℓ)).\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}(t))\;=\;\sqrt{N}\cdot\Theta(t^{\ell}),\quad u_{\ell}^{\top}G_{\ell}(t)\,u_{\ell}\;=\;\Theta\!\big(t^{2(L-\ell)}\big),\quad\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})=\Theta\!\big(t^{2(L-\ell)}\big).

Sketch. Forward propagation of a rank-deficient input through identity-skip residuals contributes σmin​(Xℓ)∝tℓ\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})\propto t^{\ell} along the canonical direction (the dead direction picks up one factor of tt per layer). Backward propagation: Gℓ=Wℓ+1⊤​Gℓ+1​Wℓ+1+(terms vanishing under canonical alignment)G_{\ell}=W_{\ell+1}^{\top}G_{\ell+1}W_{\ell+1}+(\text{terms vanishing under canonical alignment}), recursively giving GℓG_{\ell} the rate of Wℓ+1⋯WLW_{\ell+1}\cdots W_{L} which is tL−ℓt^{L-\ell} per matrix factor squared.

T3a. A–G duality (Cor. 25, theory paper).

KFAC factorises the per-layer Fisher as Fℓ≈Aℓ⊗GℓF_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}\otimes G_{\ell} with Aℓ=𝔼⁡[Xℓ−1​Xℓ−1⊤]A_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[X_{\ell-1}X_{\ell-1}^{\top}] and Gℓ=𝔼⁡[δℓ​δℓ⊤]G_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}]. Hence λmin​(Fℓ)=λmin​(Aℓ)​λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(F_{\ell})=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})\,\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}). Combining T3 with the activation-side rate σmin​(Xℓ−1)∝tℓ−1\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell-1})\propto t^{\ell-1} gives the structural correlation

λmin​(Aℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ−1)2⟹λmin+​(Gℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ)2\lambda_{\min}(A_{\ell})\;\propto\;\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell-1})^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\;\propto\;\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2}}

as a layer-local relation between the activation bottom and the Fisher-Gram bottom. This is the structural prediction tested in §4.4; it requires only that both observables read the same rank-deficient geometry, without requiring the trajectory to be canonical-aligned, which is why it survives Adam++CE.

T4. Curvature–volume rate chain (Prop. 8 + Cor. 9, theory paper).

At KL order kk, the Fisher–Riemannian sectional curvature diverges at rate Θ⁡(t−(2​k−1))\Theta(t^{-(2k-1)}) and the log-volume of the Fisher’s image scales as

logdet+(F(θ0+tu))=−2(k−1)logt+O(1)\log\det^{+}\!\big(F(\theta_{0}+tu)\big)\;=\;-2(k-1)\log t+O(1)

where det+\det^{+} is the product of strictly-positive eigenvalues. With rr independent dead directions of order kk, the volume slope is rank-multiplicative (−2​r​(k−1)​log⁡t-2r(k-1)\log t); the smallest-eigenvalue rate is rank-invariant. The multi-direction ratio test of App. B.8.2 (the logdet+\log\det^{+} slope ratio against the rank-11 baseline tracks the rank-deficit across r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\}: 1.96,3.13,3.971.96,3.13,3.97 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 vs predicted 2,3,42,3,4, across 77 configurations) is the discriminator that single-rank tests cannot access.

Definitions of the DDS observables.

At layer ℓ\ell, Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} stacks the post-activation hidden states for NN calibration samples; Gℓ∈ℝh×hG_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times h} is the per-sample-gradient outer-product Gram defined above.

  • •

    σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}): smallest singular value of XℓX_{\ell} (cheapest activation-side reading of degeneracy).

  • •

    λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}): smallest strictly positive eigenvalue of GℓG_{\ell} (Fisher-side dual via the A–G duality of T3a; “++” guards against the rank-deficient floor when n<hn<h).

  • •

    logdet+(Gℓ):=∑j:λj>0logλj\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}):=\sum_{j:\lambda_{j}>0}\log\lambda_{j}: log-volume class of the Fisher’s image, the volume-side observable in the rate chain (T4).

  • •

    eff​-​rank​(Xℓ):=exp⁡(H⁡(p1,…,ph))\mathrm{eff\text{-}rank}(X_{\ell}):=\exp\!\big(H(p_{1},\ldots,p_{h})\big) with pi=σi2/∑jσj2p_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}/\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}^{2} and HH the Shannon entropy: a soft entropy-summary of the live-direction count, ranging in [1,h][1,h]. Geometric complement to the rate chain (not derived from T1–T4) that is framework-consistent and the most testbed-robust ranker on the cells in this paper.

The framework predicts the signs of every cross-cell correlation between these observables and a complexity invariant: as the singular structure deepens, σmin\sigma_{\min} and λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) shrink (negative correlation with λ\lambda); logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) becomes more negative (more directions contribute small eigenvalues to the volume); eff​-​rank\mathrm{eff\text{-}rank} grows at the bottom-spectrum-broadening boundary because more directions carry comparable mass. The empirical §4 validates these signs on the Aoyagi closed-form testbeds and on the Nanda transformer extension.

B.3 Framing-only predictions used in the discussion

The two predictions below are referenced in the body but not directly tested in the empirical experiments of §4. They are restated here for completeness; the full assumption sets, proofs, and architectural extensions are in Shirodkar 2026.

Theorem 4 (Composition additivity; Shirodkar 2026, Thm. 30).

For a sequential stack of MLP / pre-norm residual blocks with shared dead direction, the dead-direction Fisher rate at the input of block BiB_{i} is Θ⁡(t2​∑j≥ikjbk)\Theta(t^{2\sum_{j\geq i}k_{j}^{\mathrm{bk}}}): per-block backward rates kjbkk_{j}^{\mathrm{bk}} add along the path. Pure attention chains at depth ≥4\geq 4 break this additivity via softmax cross-block coupling (Remark 32); the closed-form refinement at the per-component level is Prop. 69 of Shirodkar 2026. This theorem is the basis for the architectural extensions to rectangular widths, biases, cross-entropy with Z-loss gauge fix, and the residual-DAG / attention-chain composition results referenced as scope statements throughout §4.

Corollary 5 (Quotient Fisher rate; Shirodkar 2026, Cor. 78).

For losses invariant under a continuous Lie group GG acting on Θ\Theta, Theorem 2’s rate identity holds verbatim on the gauge quotient Θ/G\Theta/G, with the gauge orbit playing the role of a smooth singular fibre. Projected SGD on Θ/G\Theta/G realises the quotient rate (Cor. 79). Adam’s per-coordinate preconditioner is not GG-equivariant: its trajectory carries gauge-mode drift and the trajectory-rate readout is not directly applicable to Adam-class dynamics (Remark 80). This corollary scopes the trajectory-rate-readout claims of §B.8 and the Adam non-equivariance framing of the structural-correlation universality test in §4.4.

B.4 Observable computation protocols

Self-contained per-observable protocols, summarising what gets computed and at what cost.

σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) on activations (real-time cadence).

For each transformer block ℓ\ell, capture the residual-stream activation matrix Xℓ∈ℝN×hX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times h} in a single forward pass over NN calibration tokens (we use N≤1024N\leq 1024 for grokking and N=8192N=8192 at LLM scale via WikiText calibration). Compute the SVD of XℓX_{\ell}; report σmin\sigma_{\min}, σmax\sigma_{\max}, the bottom singular vector uℓresu_{\ell}^{\mathrm{res}}, and effective rank. For widths h>4096h>4096, use chunked covariance accumulation Cℓ=∑chunksXℓ⊤​XℓC_{\ell}=\sum_{\mathrm{chunks}}X_{\ell}^{\top}X_{\ell} and eigendecompose CℓC_{\ell} to recover the singular values; this keeps peak memory bounded on a single 3090. Cost: 1 forward pass per checkpoint, all layers (the per-layer SVD is post-hoc on the captured activations).

σmin\sigma_{\min} vs. the rank-aware σ(r0)\sigma_{(r_{0})}. We report the literal smallest singular value σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}). Along a singular approach the dead direction is the one decaying to zero, so it stays the smallest singular value even once it sinks below the floating-point floor, and σmin\sigma_{\min} tracks it. The rank-aware variant σ(r0)\sigma_{(r_{0})} (smallest singular value above the relative floor σmax​εmachine\sigma_{\max}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}) coincides with σmin\sigma_{\min} on the testbeds here; it is the read to prefer only when a trivial algebraic kernel sits below the geometric dead direction (e.g. the post-final-LayerNorm 𝟏\mathbf{1}-direction at σ=0\sigma=0 identically; Cor. 58), where the literal σmin\sigma_{\min} instead locks onto the non-geometric kernel. Substituting σ(r0)\sigma_{(r_{0})} on the decaying-dead-direction testbeds lowers the structural correlation, because it over-skips the below-floor dead direction in favour of a higher non-decaying one: ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σ)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma) falls from +0.83+0.83 to +0.72+0.72 on Barak and from +0.85+0.85 to +0.68+0.68 on Nanda SGD++MSE. So σmin\sigma_{\min} is the correct activation-side read for the geometric dead direction; the rank correlation stays floor-robust because σmin\sigma_{\min} and λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+} shrink together.

u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu at the σmin\sigma_{\min} direction (checkpoint cadence).

Identify the bottom singular direction u=uℓresu=u_{\ell}^{\mathrm{res}} from the activation-side σmin\sigma_{\min} step above. Compute the per-sample gradient of the loss with respect to layer-ℓ\ell pre-activations δℓ(i)=∇aℓL(i)\delta_{\ell}^{(i)}=\nabla_{a_{\ell}}L^{(i)} via one backward pass (auto-diff on the shared computation graph from the σmin\sigma_{\min} step). The directional Fisher value is u⊤​Gℓ​u=(1/n)​∑i(u⊤​δℓ(i))2u^{\top}G_{\ell}u=(1/n)\sum_{i}(u^{\top}\delta_{\ell}^{(i)})^{2}. Cost: 1 forward + 1 backward pass per (checkpoint, direction) = 1 FBP.

λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) via full eigendecomposition (periodic cadence).
11 1 The Hessian-eigenvalue-tracking lineage [Sagun et al. 2018, Ghorbani et al. 2019, Yao et al. 2020] chases primarily the top of the spectrum (sharpness) via Lanczos / Hutchinson estimators; we evaluate the same kind of estimator on the bottom of the spectrum, with the rate framework (Theorem 21) selecting the diagnostic direction without a full eigendecomposition when the structurally-determined direction is known.

Capture per-sample gradients {δℓ(i)}i=1n\{\delta_{\ell}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n} as in the u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu step but at nn samples (no fixed uu); form the empirical Gram Gℓ=(1/n)​∑iδℓ(i)​(δℓ(i))⊤∈ℝh×hG_{\ell}=(1/n)\sum_{i}\delta_{\ell}^{(i)}(\delta_{\ell}^{(i)})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times h} and eigendecompose. As a sum of outer products, GℓG_{\ell} is positive semi-definite (PSD) by construction: v⊤​Gℓ​v=(1/n)​∑i(v⊤​δℓ(i))2≥0v^{\top}G_{\ell}v=(1/n)\sum_{i}(v^{\top}\delta_{\ell}^{(i)})^{2}\geq 0 for all vv, so the theoretical λmin​(Gℓ)≥0\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell})\geq 0 always. The smallest eigenvalue is λmin\lambda_{\min}; the full spectrum {λj}\{\lambda_{j}\} exposes multiple dead directions and supports the per-layer rate validation that exercises Theorem 21’s prediction directly. Practical requirement: n/h≥100n/h\geq 100 for stable estimation; smaller nn gives CV >100%>100\% and can invert the rate-fit sign. Cost: ∼n/B\sim n/B FBPs to collect the gradient samples (where BB is batch size; e.g. for h=128h=128, n=12,800n=12{,}800, B=128B=128, that is 100100 FBP) plus O⁡(h3)O(h^{3}) eigendecomposition (small at h≤500h\leq 500, prohibitive at LLM widths).

Numerical recipe at the λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) step. Empirical Grams from few samples are rank-deficient (rank⁡(Gℓ)≤min⁡(n,h)\mathrm{rank}(G_{\ell})\leq\min(n,h)), so the smallest eigenvalues are numerically sensitive. The default in the released pipeline is Tikhonov regularization (replace GℓG_{\ell} with Gℓ+ε​IG_{\ell}+\varepsilon I before calling eigvalsh, with ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8} by convention), which guarantees all eigenvalues are ≥ε\geq\varepsilon so the solver does not return nonsense negatives from fp32 round-off. This is the right default for fp32, but it clamps all physically-smaller eigenvalues to ε\varepsilon. At fp64 the round-off floor is far below 10−810^{-8}, and we therefore switch off Tikhonov entirely and read the smallest positive eigenvalue: the literal eigvalsh minimum can be slightly negative from rank-deficient round-off, so the smallest positive eigenvalue is the numerically faithful approximation to the PSD minimum in a setting where the theoretical value approaches zero. Concretely, we discard eigenvalues whose magnitude is below the fp64 round-off floor relative to the spectral norm (∼‖G‖2⋅10−15\sim\|G\|_{2}\cdot 10^{-15}) and report the smallest above this threshold. The protocol-cost gap between the fp32+Tikhonov default and this fp64+smallest-positive recipe is |ρ|=0.10|\rho|{=}0.10 vs 0.960.96 on a Barak-width complexity-ranking sanity check.

Sample-budget gate (depth-aware n/dn/d).

The n/h≥100n/h\geq 100 rule above is the default minimum bar for rank-correlation observables. For magnitude reads at deep singular checkpoints the rule tightens with σmin\sigma_{\min} depth: at well-conditioned checkpoints (σmin\sigma_{\min} within ∼1\sim 1 OOM of σmax\sigma_{\max}) n/h≥100n/h{\geq}100 gives CV ≤0.015\leq 0.015 on λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+}; at deep singular checkpoints (σmin\sigma_{\min} several OOM below σmax\sigma_{\max}) even n/h=100n/h{=}100 retains CV ≈1\approx 1 on λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G); magnitude estimates become unrecoverable at any feasible nn, the fp-precision floor margin σmin/(σmax​εdtype)\sigma_{\min}/(\sigma_{\max}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dtype}}}) is the binding constraint. Rank-correlation observables (Spearman ρ\rho across checkpoints) are robust to this floor (rank order survives CV ∼1\sim 1 on individual magnitudes), which is why the structural correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min}) holds at ρ=+0.832±0.126\rho=+0.832\pm 0.126 on Barak Phase A across 3030 seeds even at n/D=2n/D{=}2 where slope-fits degrade. An analytical CV upper bound from first-order perturbation theory plus Davis–Kahan is CV⁡(λmin+)≤(1/N)⋅(σmax/σmin)\mathrm{CV}(\lambda_{\min}^{+})\leq(1/\sqrt{N})\cdot(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}), typically 55–10×10\times pessimistic on structured GG, much tighter than the operator-norm Wishart bound D/N⋅(σmax/σmin)2\sqrt{D/N}\cdot(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min})^{2} which is 5050–500×500\times pessimistic on the same data.

LLC via SGLD sampling (offline cadence).

External estimator from the devinterp library [Timaeus and collaborators 2024, Lau et al. 2025]; we use the tool as published. The SGLD budget is our own calibration: 44 chains ×\times (100100 burn-in +100+100 draws ×10\times 10 thinning) =4,400=4{,}400 SGLD steps, chosen as the smallest configuration passing Gelman–Rubin R^≤1.10\hat{R}\leq 1.10 and lag-1 ESS ≥25\geq 25 per chain on our testbed checkpoints, then sanity-checked against a 9×9\times-larger (40,80040{,}800 FBP) saturation budget. Each SGLD step is approximately one forward + backward pass on a calibration batch (1 FBP). Inverse temperature is set to the standard B/ln⁡BB/\ln B default. Per-task (lrSGLD,γ)(\mathrm{lr}_{\mathrm{SGLD}},\gamma) are locked via a 5×55\times 5 grid sweep at fresh checkpoints (seed 42) per testbed, selecting the single config that minimises CV subject to the R^\hat{R} + ESS gate. The per-testbed locks used by this paper, with full gate diagnostics, are tabulated in App. B.5; in summary: Aoyagi anchor (10−3,300)(10^{-3},300) at H=3,r=2H{=}3,r{=}2 seed 42; DLN-RRR (10−3,300)(10^{-3},300) at h=64,r=2h{=}64,r{=}2 seed 42; Nanda (10−3,300)(10^{-3},300) at dmodel=128d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}128 for the 55-seed re-run + width sweep (per-width locks (3⋅10−4,1000)(3\cdot 10^{-4},1000) at d=32d{=}32, (10−4,1000)(10^{-4},1000) at d=64d{=}64); Barak (10−4,100)(10^{-4},100) for the legacy v4 3030-seed run cited in §B.8, re-locked to (10−3,1000)(10^{-3},1000) under the current gate (re-run pending).

fp64 + log-space recipes for production.

The cleanup-phase precision floor on grokking trajectories can be pushed arbitrarily low for monitoring purposes without touching the training path. Two complementary recipes:

  • •

    fp64 at the measurement only. Keep training in the native precision (bf16/fp16/fp32). Before the SVD or eigendecomposition, upcast the captured activations or Gram matrix: X.to(torch.float64). At LLM widths (h≤8192h\leq 8192, N≤8192N\leq 8192), fp64 SVD costs ∼1\sim 1 s and ∼260\sim 260 MB extra memory on a single 3090, negligible compared to the training-step cost, and removes the ∼10−7\sim 10^{-7} fp32 precision floor entirely.

  • •

    Log-space accumulation. For u⊤​G​u=∑i(u⊤​δi)2/nu^{\top}Gu=\sum_{i}(u^{\top}\delta_{i})^{2}/n the summands span orders of magnitude near the singular minimum; a naive sum loses small contributions to cancellation. Use torch.logsumexp on {2​log⁡|u⊤​δi|}\{2\log|u^{\top}\delta_{i}|\} to compute log⁡(n​u⊤​G​u)\log(nu^{\top}Gu) in log-space, then expose u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu as its exponential when needed. For single-direction probes the sharpness ratio is best reported in log-space directly.

Both recipes are a measurement-pass cost, not a training cost, and are applied uniformly in the released code at the SVD / backward-capture call sites.

B.5 LLC SGLD calibration audit

The cost-and-comparison story between DDS and calibrated LLC depends on what the LLC numbers represent on each testbed. We document what is calibrated where, the calibration gate, and the per-cell locks, so the reader can assess the LLC baseline at the cell-level granularity reviewers typically ask for.

Calibration gate.

Every paper-claimable LLC reading uses a 44-chain ×\times (100CLOSE(100 burn-in +100+100 draws × 10\times\,10 thin)) =4,400=4{,}400 SGLD steps per call (the “recommended budget”), with per-task (lrsgld,γ)(\mathrm{lr}_{\mathrm{sgld}},\gamma) locked via a 5×55\times 5 grid sweep against the acceptance gate Gelman–Rubin R^≤1.10\hat{R}\leq 1.10 and lag-1 ESS ≥25\geq 25 per chain, with min-CV selection among accepted configurations. Inverse temperature uses devinterp.utils.default_nbeta=B/ln⁡B=B/\ln B. A 9×9\times saturation gate (40,80040{,}800 SGLD steps) confirms the locked config is operating in the saturation regime. Calibrations that fail the gate are not paper-claimable; they are flagged below.

Reading the calibration matrix.

On the Nanda width sweep the four widths each have their own gate-passing 5×55\times 5-grid lock with a 9×9\times saturation check, so that head-to-head is fully per-cell calibrated. On the closed-form RLCT testbeds (Aoyagi 2005 anchor, Aoyagi 2024 DLN) the LLC uses a single lock that is itself fully calibrated at H=3,r=2H{=}3,r{=}2 (resp. h=64,rd=2h{=}64,\mathrm{rd}{=}2): a 5×55\times 5 grid selected by the R^≤1.10\hat{R}\leq 1.10 and per-chain ESS ≥25\geq 25 gate with min-CV, with the 9×9\times saturation check passing (R^=0.996\hat{R}{=}0.996, ESSmin=70.9{}_{\min}{=}70.9, CV=0.014=0.014, saturated). That lock is then transferred across the sweep. The per-cell recalibration audit below confirms that transferring the fully-calibrated lock, rather than recalibrating every cell, is the most defensible single choice and leaves the rank-based readings unchanged.

DLN-RRR per-cell calibration audit.

To test whether per-cell recalibration on the DLN 2424-cell sweep (h∈{16,20,24,32,64,128}h\in\{16,20,24,32,64,128\}, r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\}) eliminates the documented across-hh drift, we ran two further calibrations alongside the original transfer and compared all three on the same trained models.

All three calibrations show substantial drift across hh; per-cell recalibration does not eliminate it, and the most aggressive recalibration (free-grid min-CV) actually amplifies it. The drift is therefore structural to local LLC at this testbed, not an artefact of any single calibration choice, consistent with the local-LLC-at-w⋆w^{\star} vs global-RLCT distinction of Lau et al. 2025: the global RLCT is constant in hh above saturation while the local-LLC retains a depth-dependent reading by design. The Aoyagi closed-form is the global RLCT; SGLD-based estimators measure local LLC. The min-CV selection criterion biases toward tighter-chain (over-localised) configurations: the free-grid lock typically picks γ∈{300,1000}\gamma\in\{300,1000\}, probing too small a neighbourhood of w⋆w^{\star} and yielding ∼100×\sim\!100{\times} smaller absolute LLC than the transfer with wider relative drift. The γ=100\gamma{=}100 controlled recalibration, varying only lrsgld\mathrm{lr}_{\mathrm{sgld}}, sits between the two and is the most defensible single choice we examined; all 2424 cells lock at lrsgld=10−3\mathrm{lr}_{\mathrm{sgld}}{=}10^{-3} (the upper end of the grid), 22/2422/24 pass the 9×9{\times} saturation check.

Material consequence for paper claims.

The paper’s DLN-RRR head-to-head reads cross-cell Spearman |ρ||\rho| between LLC and DDS observables (§4.4), which is rank-invariant to LLC magnitude. All three calibrations produce the same cell-level ordering (LLC monotonically increases with hh at fixed rr and decreases with rr at fixed hh), so the paper’s |ρ||\rho| readings are unaffected by the calibration-magnitude question. The cost comparison (∼130×\sim\!130{\times} cheaper than calibrated LLC) is also unaffected. We retain the transfer lock as the canonical reading because (i) it is the publicly-documented protocol in Hoogland et al. 2024, (ii) it produces the narrowest of the three across-hh drifts, and (iii) the paper’s claims do not depend on absolute LLC magnitudes.

Closed-form recovery on the Aoyagi anchor (full standard).

The Aoyagi 2005 anchor admits a stricter calibration check than rank-tracking: whether calibrated LLC recovers the closed-form λ\lambda in magnitude. Under a target-λ\lambda calibration at full standard (5×\times5 grid, R^≤1.10\hat{R}\leq 1.10 and per-chain ESS ≥25\geq 25 gate, 9×9\times saturation confirmed; lock (lrsgld,γ)=(10−3,5)(\mathrm{lr}_{\mathrm{sgld}},\gamma){=}(10^{-3},5), R^=1.00\hat{R}{=}1.00, ESSmin=51{}_{\min}{=}51), calibrated LLC recovers λ\lambda at 99%99\% mean across the 1414 cells (range 6161–103%103\%; e.g. λ^LLC=8.98\hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{LLC}}{=}8.98 vs closed-form 99, and 25.7925.79 vs 2525). Magnitude recovery is a separate statement from rank-tracking: the same per-cell values give a cross-cell Spearman vs λ\lambda of only 0.7170.717, because near-tied λ\lambda values reshuffle ranks under sub-percent measurement error. The closed-form magnitude recovery is the trustworthy ground-truth check; the cross-cell Spearman is the weaker, sanity-gate reading.

B.6 Dead-Direction Signatures (DDS): closed-form RLCT anchor for the universality + cost claims

This section anchors the broader DDS narrative on closed-form RLCT ground truth. The narrative has three layered claims:

  1. 1.

    Universality. The structural correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min}) holds across architectures, optimizers, losses, and grok-vs-no-grok regimes (Section B.8.2: ρ≥+0.75\rho\geq{+}0.75 on canonical bridge, Barak SGD++MSE, Nanda SGD++MSE, Nanda AdamW++CE).

  2. 2.

    Cost ordering. DDS is 10310^{3}–10410^{4} times cheaper than calibrated LLC at every checkpoint on the small-model testbeds evaluated here (range extends to 105×10^{5}\times on the longer Pile-LM chain): σmin\sigma_{\min} via SVD ∼1\sim 1 ms; λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) via full eigendecomposition ∼14\sim 14 ms; logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) from the same eigendecomposition is free; locked-config SGLD-LLC at the converged checkpoint ∼25\sim 25 s on small models, ∼5\sim 5 min on Pile-LM (Sections B.7, B.8, B.6).

  3. 3.

    Quantitative anchor (this section). On the rectangular 2-matrix RRR family with closed-form RLCT (Aoyagi & Watanabe 2005), DDS rate-chain observables rank-track the analytical λ\lambda across the 1414 anchor cells at cross-cell |ρ|∈[0.95,0.98]|\rho|\in[0.95,0.98]. On the square 3-matrix DLN-RRR family (Aoyagi 2024 + Lau et al. 2023 App. I) the analytical λ\lambda is constant above saturation (200=d2/2200=d^{2}/2 in both hh and rank deficit), and DDS observables track that constancy while calibrated LLC drifts; cross-cell ρ\rho vs λ\lambda there is a tied-rank artifact that carries no rank-tracking signal. The transformer extension below (Nanda modular-addition width sweep, 44 widths × 30\times\,30 seeds, 101101 grokked) shows the same observables track dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} at |ρ|∈[0.62,0.96]|\rho|\in[0.62,0.96] with the framework-predicted sign on every observable.

The three Dead-Direction Signatures (DDS) observables are all framework-derived: σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) (activation-side dual), λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) (rate), and logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) (volume). The two RRR families chosen here remove LLC-calibration drift as a confound: λ\lambda is closed-form (no SGLD), and the testbeds are small enough that per-testbed LLC calibration is tractable (we run a 5×\times5 grid + 9×\times saturation gate at one cell per testbed, lock the result, and re-run the sweep at the locked config).

Framework status of each observable.

The rate-chain observables (λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) and logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G)) are derived from Theorem 2 (Fisher decay Θ⁡(t2​(k−1))\Theta(t^{2(k-1)}) at the singular minimum) and Corollary 9 (volume scaling). The framework predicts negative cross-cell correlation with Aoyagi λ\lambda: more singular →\to smaller Fisher eigenvalue →\to smaller volume of the Fisher’s image. σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) is the activation-side dual via Corollary 25; on a dimension-fixed boundary layer it reads the truth’s rank (positive sign across the grid).

Setup: Aoyagi 2005 anchor (rectangular 2-matrix RRR, 2D grid).

Sign structure follows the rate chain.

Aoyagi λ\lambda is roughly the dimension of the singular fiber, so larger λ\lambda means more degenerate parameter manifold. The Fisher and volume observables decay together as the singularity deepens (Theorem 2, Corollary 9): λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) measures the sharpest direction (rate Θ⁡(t2​(k−1))\Theta(t^{2(k-1)})), logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) measures the volume of the Fisher’s image, and the two are different rungs of the same chain (ρ>0\rho>0 between them across the grid; ρ<0\rho<0 for each vs Aoyagi λ\lambda). σmin​(h2)\sigma_{\min}(h_{2})’s positive sign is the truth-rank readout: at the output activation (dimension fixed at N=5N{=}5), the smallest singular value is set by the truth’s rank rather than by parameter-manifold dimensionality (rank-1 truth ⇒\Rightarrow output is rank-1 ⇒\Rightarrow σmin​(h2)→0\sigma_{\min}(h_{2})\to 0; full-rank truth ⇒\Rightarrow σmin​(h2)>0\sigma_{\min}(h_{2})>0). Higher rr increases both Aoyagi λ\lambda and σmin​(h2)\sigma_{\min}(h_{2}), hence the positive correlation. The interior-layer counterpart σmin​(h1)\sigma_{\min}(h_{1}) is dominated by dead-direction descent and reads with the opposite sign. Calibrated LLC for this anchor is reported in the baseline comparison below; under a target-λ\lambda calibration it recovers the closed-form λ\lambda at ∼99%\sim\!99\% mean across the 1414 cells (App. B.5).

Layer-choice caveat.

The hh-extensive logdet+\log\det^{+} summand at the interior layer h1h_{1} (dimh1=H\dim h_{1}=H, varies across cells) gives ρ=−0.103\rho{=}{-}0.103; at fixed λ\lambda the values differ between (H=2,r=2)(H{=}2,r{=}2) and (H=4,r=1)(H{=}4,r{=}1) by a factor proportional to hh. The same observable on h2h_{2} (output, dimension N=5N{=}5 everywhere) does not share the confound and reads −0.947-0.947. When picking DDS observables for cross-cell ranking on RRR-style grids, prefer the dimension-fixed boundary layer for sharpness-style observables.

Noise-level robustness.

Aoyagi λ\lambda is asymptotic in n→∞n\to\infty and does not depend on the additive noise σ\sigma; the DDS observables do depend on σ\sigma at finite nn, so the natural robustness check is whether the cell-ordering survives a σ\sigma sweep. We re-ran the full 14-cell grid at σ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2}\sigma\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\} (210210 runs total) and report Spearman ρ\rho versus Aoyagi λ\lambda at each σ\sigma:

The σmin​(h2)\sigma_{\min}(h_{2}) reading is σ\sigma-invariant (range 0.0000.000): a structural rank-correlation depending only on the integer rank-deficit pattern. The Fisher-side observables (λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+}, logdet+\log\det^{+}) drift slightly with σ\sigma: at higher noise the trained w∗w^{*} sits further from the singular locus, softening the Fisher-decay signal. The high-noise drop on logdet+(Gh2)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) at σ=0.2\sigma{=}0.2 (−0.723-0.723) is the largest cross-σ\sigma swing in the table, in the predicted direction: more noise →\to less complete approach to the singular locus →\to less negative logdet+\log\det^{+} at fixed λ\lambda →\to rank correlation softens.

Per-cell rank consistency vs LLC at fixed (H,r)(H,r).

A common reviewer concern on cross-cell Spearman read on a structurally varying grid is that the cross-cell |ρ|=0.95|\rho|{=}0.95 headline is the easiest possible setup for a monotone observable: cells differ in (H,r)(H,r) which drives both DDS and LLC, and any sane observable will rank-track such structural variation. The orthogonal cut is the per-cell test: at fixed (H,r)(H,r), do DDS observables and calibrated LLC agree on the within-cell ranking of the 55 seeds ×\times 33 noise levels = 1515 runs? Within a cell, analytical Aoyagi λ\lambda is constant by construction (rank ties on the y-axis), so the test is necessarily against LLC or against val_loss as a realised-difficulty proxy. Across the 1414 cells of the Aoyagi 2005 anchor at the boundary layer h2h_{2}, the per-cell Spearman ρ\rho vs locked-config LLC has medians −0.40-0.40 for λmin+​(Gh2)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) (IQR [−0.60,−0.07][-0.60,-0.07], 0%0\% of cells positive), −0.30-0.30 for logdet+(Gh2)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) (IQR [−0.60,+0.05][-0.60,+0.05], 29%29\% positive), and +0.10+0.10 for σmin​(h2)\sigma_{\min}(h_{2}) (IQR [−0.22,+0.67][-0.22,+0.67], 50%50\% positive). The Fisher-side rate-chain observables (λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+}, logdet+\log\det^{+}) carry the framework-predicted negative sign within cells (DDS smaller ↔\leftrightarrow LLC larger, in the same direction the cross-cell test reports) at modest but non-trivial magnitude. The within-cell magnitude (|ρ||\rho| medians 0.300.30–0.400.40) is much smaller than the cross-cell magnitude (|ρ|=0.95|\rho|{=}0.95), as expected: cross-cell variation tracks structural complexity differences (large signal); within-cell variation tracks realised-fluctuation differences at fixed structural complexity (small signal). The activation-side σmin\sigma_{\min} does not carry significant within-cell signal vs LLC, consistent with its truth-rank-readout role rather than rate-chain role at this layer. A separate per-cell test against val_loss as a realised-difficulty proxy gives non-trivial within-cell tracking: λmin+​(Gh2)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) at ρmedian=+0.80\rho_{\mathrm{median}}=+0.80 (mean +0.80+0.80, std 0.0000.000), logdet+(Gh2)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) at ρmedian=+0.79\rho_{\mathrm{median}}=+0.79 (std 0.0000.000); the near-zero cross-cell std comes from the 33-level σ\sigma-noise sweep driving both DDS and val_loss in lockstep within each cell. The within-cell test is therefore weaker on the headline magnitude (cross-cell dominates) but the rate-chain observables track in the right direction in both LLC and val_loss readings.
