Any monotone observable of (H,r)(H,r) should rank-track λ\lambda tightly on such a grid, so the cross-cell test functions as a passing-bar for monotone-in-complexity observables rather than as a discriminating test between framework-derived and ad hoc choices. The discriminating contribution of the framework appears in a structural prediction the cross-cell test cannot resolve: at any singular minimum with rank-deficit rr, logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope scales linearly in rr while λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope is rr-invariant. The slope ratio against the rank-11 baseline equals rr, a strict, prefactor-free quantitative identity. Single-rank spectral monitors and (H,r)(H,r) proxies are rank-blind and cannot produce this prediction. We measure the ratio tracking the rank-deficit across r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\} (1.96,3.13,3.971.96,3.13,3.97 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 vs predicted 2,3,42,3,4) on 77 configurations spanning L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\}, D∈{20,50}D\in\{20,50\}, full and mini-batch SGD (§4.2). The cross-cell |ρ|=0.95|\rho|{=}0.95–0.980.98 on Aoyagi is the passing-bar; the rank-multi ratio is the discriminator.

The two readouts answer different questions on this axis.

The within-cell test on the 2424-cell DLN sweep has N=5N{=}5 per cell (seeds only, no σ\sigma sweep), so per-cell Spearman is noisy at this nn. Magnitudes are weaker on the 3-matrix DLN-RRR than on the 2-matrix Aoyagi anchor (the cross-cell ranking task is harder when the model has more layers between the bottleneck and the readout, and the hh-extensive normalisation of the rate-chain summands compresses dynamic range across cells of different width); the prediction direction holds throughout.

Cost ordering.

Per-checkpoint observable cost on these problems: σmin\sigma_{\min} via SVD ∼1\sim\!1 ms; λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G) via full eigendecomposition ∼14\sim\!14 ms; logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G) from the same eigendecomposition is free; locked-config SGLD-LLC at the converged checkpoint ∼25\sim\!25 s/cell. The DDS suite runs at 10310^{3}–104×10^{4}\times lower per-call cost on these testbeds, sitting in a different cadence regime from the SGLD chain. On Aoyagi-style closed-form λ\lambda the rank-tracking is tight; for posterior-Bayesian readings (singular fluctuations, WAIC, developmental-stage trajectories) calibrated LLC remains the canonical tool.

Scope and limitations.

Two RRR families with closed-form RLCT do not certify that DDS rate-chain observables generalise to deep nonlinear models, where the correspondence between rank degeneracy and λ\lambda is not analytical. The grokking and TMS sections establish the qualitative correspondence in the nonlinear setting; this section adds the quantitative anchor on the linear closed-form case. The width-axis disagreement between calibrated LLC and Aoyagi λ\lambda on the 24-cell sweep is reported as a calibration-discipline observation: the calibrated LLC is the local read at w⋆w^{\star} that the locked SGLD config is designed to deliver, while Aoyagi λ\lambda is the global RLCT, and the distinction is made explicit in [Lau et al. 2025]. Specific reproducibility caveats: the anchor sweeps the 2D (H,r)(H,r) grid (14 valid cells with λ∈[9,25]\lambda\in[9,25]) at fixed M=10M{=}10, N=5N{=}5, with σ\sigma-robustness checked at σ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2}\sigma\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}. The closed-form Σ\Sigma-subset selector in Aoyagi 2024 is implemented by brute-force enumeration over the 2L+12^{L+1} subsets (16 at L=3L{=}3, ≤1024\leq 1024 at L≤9L\leq 9); a closed-form selector for general (𝑯,r)(\bm{H},r) does not appear in the original paper. What LLC retains beyond DDS is its Bayesian-WBIC interpretability and the explicit integration over the local posterior [Lau et al. 2025], plus its trajectory-shape signature during training: the developmental-stage plateaus and jumps reported by [Hoogland et al. 2024] are not currently replicated by DDS observables. The narrow claim made by this section is the quantitative anchor: on closed-form RLCT testbeds, DDS rate-chain observables carry the framework-predicted negative sign at |ρ|∈[0.95,0.98]|\rho|\in[0.95,0.98] on the dimension-fixed boundary layer.

Reading the relative std column.

The rel-std numbers split into two regimes. The bounded-range observable logdet+(G)∈\log\det^{+}(G)\in a sum-of-bounded-positives range is linear-scale; its 3535–185%185\% rel-std is meaningful per-seed variability of the converged geometry (the high end is logdet+(Gh1)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{1}}), whose near-zero mean at d=32d{=}32 inflates the linear ratio; logdet+(Gh2)\log\det^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) at 35%35\% is the clean bounded-range reading). The smallest-eigenvalue observables (σmin\sigma_{\min}, λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), Hessian trace/sharpness) span orders of magnitude across seeds and widths, so linear-scale rel-std overstates the spread: σmin​(h1)\sigma_{\min}(h_{1}) at d=32d{=}32 shows linear rel-std ∼200%\sim 200\%, normal for singular-minimum readings whose underlying spread is multiplicative. The Spearman ρ\rho column is rank-invariant either way, which is why it recovers signal at |ρ|=0.91|\rho|{=}0.91 on λmin+​(Gh2)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{2}}) despite a linear rel-std of 447%447\%. Per-cell point estimates of the smallest-eigenvalue observables should be reported in log-space or as ratios across widths; logdet+\log\det^{+} is quotable as a linear mean ±\pm std.

The LLC width-flatness is not a budget artefact.

The LLC is reported as a posterior mean λ^\hat{\lambda} with two associated dispersions: a within-cell SGLD std (the SGLD chain’s reported std⁡(λ^)\mathrm{std}(\hat{\lambda}) at one seed) and an across-seed std (the std of the per-seed λ^\hat{\lambda} values at fixed width). To check whether the rank-flat LLC vs dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} reading is an under-sampled SGLD posterior rather than a genuine width-flatness, we re-ran 55 seeds at d=128d{=}128 at a 9×9\times budget (44 chains × 200\times\,200 burnin × 100\times\,100 draws × 90\times\,90 thin, 36,80036{,}800 total SGLD steps vs the protocol’s 4,4004{,}400). The within-cell SGLD std falls by 1.50×1.50\times (from 15.915.9 to 10.610.6), consistent with the 8.4≈2.9×\sqrt{8.4}\approx 2.9\times upper bound under independent draws and indicating the protocol budget already sits in the saturation regime for a single chain. The across-seed std, however, falls by only 1.05×1.05\times (from 80.180.1 to 75.975.9): the LLC dispersion at this width is dominated by per-seed initialisation variance rather than SGLD measurement variance. (The DDS observables (σmin\sigma_{\min}, λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), logdet+(G)\log\det^{+}(G)) are computed from a single forward pass per checkpoint; they have no SGLD budget knob and are unaffected by this re-run.) A longer SGLD budget per cell is therefore not the missing ingredient for dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} ranking on Nanda AdamW++CE; what is missing for sharp width discrimination is an external mechanism reducing the across-seed LLC spread (e.g., per-seed-conditioned LLC, or a different calibration cell where init-variance is smaller relative to width-variance). The DDS observables, by contrast, already separate the widths at |ρ|≥0.62|\rho|\geq 0.62 across all 101101 grokked cells.

This recovers the framework prediction on a transformer testbed where calibrated LLC, at this calibration budget and within the per-seed init-variance floor reported above, is rank-flat in width. DDS observables at ∼15\sim 15 ms per checkpoint separate the widths cleanly, including across 55–1515 orders of magnitude on Fisher-side readouts. Both signals report on the same singular geometry; DDS reads it at lower per-cell variance and lower compute. The closed-form Aoyagi anchor (§4.1) and the Nanda width sweep extend along the same axis: closed-form ground truth on the analytic testbeds, scope-extension on a non-linear transformer.

B.7 Toy Model of Superposition: a third phase-transition benchmark

To verify the cost–sharpness ranking generalises beyond grokking, we run the same observable suite on the Toy Model of Superposition [Elhage et al. 2022], trained with Adam ++ importance-weighted MSE on sparse inputs (din=6d_{\mathrm{in}}{=}6, dhid=2d_{\mathrm{hid}}{=}2, sparsity 0.9990.999, importance decay 0.850.85). TMS exhibits sharp phase transitions at which features shift between monosemantic and polysemantic representations as the hidden geometry reorganises. On a 2020 k-step Adam trajectory the main transition occurs at step ∼250\sim 250:

All three observable families (variance-side σmin\sigma_{\min}, Fisher-side λmin​(G)\lambda_{\min}(G) and direction-probed u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu, Bayesian LLC) detect the transition. The A–G duality (Corollary 25) holds at this small-model scale: u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu along σmin\sigma_{\min} and λmin​(G)\lambda_{\min}(G) agree to within an order of magnitude throughout training. Scope: TMS uses Adam++MSE; the table above is a static pre/post sharpness comparison (qualitative phase-detection), not a quantitative trajectory-rate validation. The trajectory-rate scope under Adam-class optimizers is governed by Remark 80 (Adam’s diagonal preconditioner is non-equivariant under continuous loss symmetries; for MSE the residual non-equivariance is bounded but non-zero); the multi-seed parametric rate validation below uses canonical-aligned freeze-probe and is the quantitative-rate test. Per-checkpoint costs: σmin∼1\sigma_{\min}\sim 1 ms; λmin​(G)\lambda_{\min}(G) full eigendecomposition ∼14\sim 14 ms; LLC ∼595\sim 595 ms; the cost ordering σmin≪λmin​(G)≪LLC\sigma_{\min}\ll\lambda_{\min}(G)\ll\mathrm{LLC} matches the ordering at larger scale (Appendix B.8); absolute ratios depend on h,Nh,N and the calibration budget. This confirms the observable-cost ordering across three benchmarks (modular addition / Nanda, sparse parity / Barak, and TMS).

Both configurations show the same qualitative pattern: ρ\rho rises with sparsity, peaking at S=0.9S{=}0.9 (ρ≈+0.84\rho\approx+0.84 on both grids), and flips sign at the dense limit S=0.05S{=}0.05 where the network is in feature-formation rather than dead-direction descent. The Chen-anchor F=6F{=}6, H=2H{=}2 reproduces the F=20F{=}20, H=5H{=}5 shape without offset, the bridge prediction is robust to TMS’s geometric parameterisation, not a coincidence of the legacy width choice. Phase note: across all 2020 k-step runs the σmin​(W)\sigma_{\min}(W) trajectory is monotone build (no descent segment with ≥5\geq 5 checkpoints recovered by the auto-segmenter); the ρ\rho above is the build-phase rank correlation, not a post-grok measurement. This is consistent with TMS’s feature-formation dynamics, features build up into superposed polytopes, the network does not subsequently prune them within the 2020 k-step horizon, and the structural prediction is satisfied during build before the trajectory’s prune phase becomes accessible. The TMS sweep is reported here as a third diagnostic anchor for the bridge correlation, complementing the canonical-bridge analytic limit (ρ=+1.000\rho{=}+1.000) and the Barak SGD++MSE Phase A result (ρ=+0.832±0.126\rho{=}+0.832\pm 0.126).

B.8 Trajectory observables on grokking

The framework’s trajectory rate-readout is scoped by three preconditions: canonical alignment, theorem-compatible preconditioner, asymptotic approach. Three optimisers satisfy all three on canonical-bridge testbeds: SGD on GG-invariant metrics (the quotient-rate corollary of Shirodkar 2026); Shampoo full-batch; KFAC++KL-clip full-batch [Martens and Grosse 2015]. We track the dead-direction observable suite at the per-benchmark checkpoint cadence (Nanda every 500500 steps, Barak every 20002000; see setups below) on two standard grokking benchmarks [Power et al. 2022, grokking on algorithmic tasks introduced by]: Nanda modular addition [Nanda et al. 2023, 1-block transformer, AdamW+CE;], out of regime for the trajectory rate-readout because Adam’s diagonal preconditioner is non-equivariant under CE’s logit-shift symmetry; and Barak sparse parity [Barak et al. 2022, 2-hidden MLP, SGD+MSE;], in regime. 3030 seeds each. Both regimes grok reliably (30/3030/30 on Nanda at step 6000±6006000\pm 600; 30/3030/30 on Barak at 7100±26007100\pm 2600); Mann–Whitney UU tests confirm pre/post separation (p<10−3p<10^{-3}) for all three Fisher/activation observables on both setups.

Phase-detection and the geometric/algorithmic split.

Across the 3030-seed canonical Barak run, σmin​(X1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{1}) and u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu along the dead direction descend through ∼6\sim\!6 orders of magnitude across the val_acc-anchored phases pre-grok / at-grok / cleanup. Both observables require fp6464 + no-Tikhonov + smallest-positive eigenvalue; fp3232+Tikhonov collapses cross-checkpoint |ρ||\rho| from 0.960.96 to 0.100.10 (numerical-recipe details in §B.4). The “grokking event” separates into two distinct transitions: algorithmic (val-acc →1\to 1, circuit discovered) and geometric (θ\theta approaches the singular minimum). On Nanda these are synchronous (Adam++CE produces drift rather than approach in the gauge kernel); on Barak they are separated by 55–1010k steps as weight decay pulls θ\theta toward the singular minimum, with u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu dropping per-seed-geomean 8.7⋅105×8.7\cdot 10^{5}\times (Tab. 2). Both post-grok minima sit on continuous invariance orbits (CE logit shift ++ ReLU rescaling on Nanda; ReLU rescaling on Barak); weight decay pulls θ\theta toward the minimum-norm point on the orbit, a singular minimum of the quotient dynamics so the directional Fisher decay theorem of Shirodkar 2026applies.

Trajectory-rate slope on Barak.

On Barak Phase A, the rank-correlation reading is ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)=+0.832±0.126\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min})=+0.832\pm 0.126 across 30/3030/30 seeds (§B.8.2). The framework’s quantitative magnitude prediction ∂log⁡u⊤​G​u/∂log⁡σmin=2\partial\log u^{\top}Gu/\partial\log\sigma_{\min}=2 requires a measurable Phase A: σmin​(Xh1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}}) at the start of the post-grok descent above the floating-point floor by enough orders of magnitude that the descent develops a fittable power-law shape within the checkpointing cadence. Whether this holds depends on (ntrain,checkpoint cadence)(n_{\mathrm{train}},\text{checkpoint cadence}) jointly. The u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu readout here is the back-propagated loss-gradient covariance, the K-FAC G-factor of the bridge factorisation, which equals the population Fisher rate only inside the asymptotic window for a well-specified configuration (Remark 4); under squared-error loss a residual prefactor can give a clean fit at a shifted exponent, so a slope is interpretable as the rate only after the regime is checked. At the canonical setup (ntrain=1000n_{\mathrm{train}}{=}1000, n/D=33n/D{=}33, save_every =2000=2000 steps), the slope-22 prediction is satisfied. Four of five seeds give x¯=2.06±0.20\bar{x}=2.06\pm 0.20 (R2∈[0.87,0.97]R^{2}\in[0.87,0.97]), with σmin​(Xh1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}}) descending gradually from ∼10−1\sim\!10^{-1} at training start to ∼10−3\sim\!10^{-3} at val-acc grok (∼6\sim\!6k steps) and onward to ∼10−14\sim\!10^{-14} over the next 200200k steps (a measurable Phase A). One seed (342) is an outlier: its σmin\sigma_{\min} minimum is reached at step 80,00080{,}000 rather than near training end, and the resulting Phase A slope is 0.360.36 at R2=0.25R^{2}=0.25. The early tmint_{\min} indicates a non-asymptotic Phase A and suggests a multi-basin structure on Barak that warrants independent investigation, outside the scope of this paper. The reliability gate of §B.4 confirms the precondition that matters for the squared-error readout: the per-layer Fisher is full-rank across Phase A on every canonical seed (eff​_​rank​(Gh1)≈320\mathrm{eff\_rank}(G_{h_{1}})\approx 320–345345 of 500500), so the slope reads a localised dead-direction descent of 1414–2121 orders of magnitude in λmin\lambda_{\min} rather than the rank-11 residual-prefactor collapse that would fit a shifted exponent at clean R2R^{2}. The four in-regime seeds carry the descent; seed 342 is the short-window read above (R2=0.25R^{2}=0.25).

Higher-n/Dn/D regime: Phase A compresses below resolvable step-cadence.

A natural follow-up question is whether the slope-22 prediction holds more cleanly at higher n/Dn/D. We re-ran 55 seeds at n/D∈{167,833}n/D\in\{167,833\} (ntrain∈{5000,25000}n_{\mathrm{train}}\in\{5000,25000\}) for 240240k steps each. All 10/1010/10 grokked. A directed fine-cadence probe (save_every =50=50, first 66k steps, 22 seeds per setting) shows what happens during the geometric event:

ntrain=5000n_{\mathrm{train}}{=}5000 (n/D=167n/D{=}167) 1,250−1,3001{,}250{-}1{,}300 ⋅10−3→⋅10−71\!\cdot\!10^{-3}\to 8\!\cdot\!10^{-7} in 200–350 steps 33 OOM in ∼350\sim 350 steps, then plateau

At higher n/Dn/D, the geometric event compresses from ∼200\sim\!200k steps (canonical) to ≤350\leq 350 steps, with the bulk of the descent inside a single 5050-step checkpoint window. Per-seed slope fits over the resolved descent (5 ckpts where the data permits) span 0.390.39 to 1.421.42 at R2∈[0.21,0.68]R^{2}\in[0.21,0.68], not interpretable as the framework’s predicted exponent, but also not a refutation: the descent is too fast to fit any rate at these cadences. Even 5050-step resolution leaves 11–55 ckpts during the actual descent. The slope-22 test is not applicable in this regime because the geometric trajectory exits the asymptotic-descent window faster than measurement can capture, regardless of the prediction’s truth value.

The grokking transition at higher n/Dn/D becomes a near-discontinuous event in step-time: as the data-richness ratio n/Dn/D grows, the optimization dynamics complete the geometric collapse in increasingly few steps, eventually concentrating the entire singular-approach into a window indistinguishable from a step-discontinuity at any practical save cadence. The rate prediction is asymptotic in the geometric variable σmin\sigma_{\min}; any trajectory whose σmin\sigma_{\min} descends through a measurable range exposes it to test. On Barak with canonical n/D=33n/D{=}33 that range is traversed over ∼200\sim\!200k steps, allowing the slope to be fit at standard checkpoint cadence; the L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\} noisy bridge family (§4.2) tests the same prediction across additional axes (depth, width, batch mode, initialization).

Scope summary.

The slope-22 prediction holds at canonical Barak (n/D=33n/D{=}33, save_every =2,000=2{,}000) on 4/54/5 seeds with the seed-342 caveat above; the structural rank-correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)=+0.83±0.13\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min})=+0.83\pm 0.13 holds across all 3030 canonical seeds independently of the cadence question. The same volume-side prediction is tested independently across the L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\} noisy-bridge family at x¯=2.034±0.055\bar{x}=2.034\pm 0.055 (77 cells; §4.2), exercising depth, width, batch mode, and initialization simultaneously. The two readings are convergent: the slope-22 prediction holds across a non-trivial real-network testbed (Barak), a multi-layer testbed under realistic Gaussian noise (the bridge family), and the analytic limit (L=2L{=}2 canonical bridge); the bridge family additionally varies depth, width, batch mode, and initialization (§B.8.2).

Re-locking Barak to (10−3,1000)(10^{-3},1000) under the current gate is documented in App. B.5; the paper’s Barak claims use ρ\rho between two DDS observables and so are unaffected by the lock change.

Compute cost per checkpoint.

In FBP units: σmin\sigma_{\min} is one forward pass + per-layer activation SVD; u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu at the σmin\sigma_{\min} direction is +1+1 FBP; full GℓG_{\ell} eigendecomposition is ∼n/d\sim n/d FBPs with n≥100​dn\geq 100\,d; LLC at our recommended SGLD budget is 4,4004{,}400 FBPs. Wall-clock numbers on a single RTX 3090 are reported in App. B.8.1.

Sharpness statistics.

For each observable, sharpness is the ratio of pre-grok to post-grok median values across the 30 seeds. Pre-grok window: training steps before the seed-mean grok step, excluding the immediate transition. Post-grok window: 5,000+ steps after the seed-mean grok step (long enough to reach the observable plateau). Mann–Whitney UU test on the per-seed pre/post observable distributions confirms significant separation (p<10−3p<10^{-3}) for σmin\sigma_{\min}, u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu, and λmin​(G)\lambda_{\min}(G) on both setups; LLC’s significance is marginal on the Nanda setup (p≈0.05p\approx 0.05) and significant on Barak (p<10−3p<10^{-3}), consistent with the smaller LLC sharpness ratio.

Robust-statistics reporting.

The cleanup-window distributions are heavy-tailed log-normal across seeds: at step 20,00020{,}000 on Barak the per-seed σmin\sigma_{\min} spans 2.6⋅10−92.6\cdot 10^{-9} to 1.2⋅10−51.2\cdot 10^{-5}, ∼4\sim 4 orders of magnitude. For ratio-scaled quantities with this dispersion, arithmetic mean ±\pm std is dominated by individual tail seeds and is not the appropriate centre. Table 3 reports geometric mean (with bootstrap 95%95\% CI on the geomean, 1,0001{,}000 resamples), median (with Q25,Q75\mathrm{Q}_{25},\mathrm{Q}_{75} as IQR), and arithmetic mean±\pmstd for legacy comparison. The order-of-magnitude story above is unchanged; cell magnitudes in cleanup-row Barak shrink by ∼8×\sim\!8\times (σmin\sigma_{\min}) to ∼300×\sim\!300\times (u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu) when the geomean is used in place of the legacy arithmetic mean.

Two cost columns are worth separating, because the observables are not independent, the u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu probe uses the direction produced by the σmin\sigma_{\min} SVD, so running u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu by itself without σmin\sigma_{\min} is ill-defined on the paper’s pipeline.

Reading the table. The assembled column is the end-to-end wall-clock to produce that observable on a checkpoint using the paper’s recipe; the marginal column is the additional cost on top of the prior step. The u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu probe reuses the bottom singular vector from the σmin\sigma_{\min} SVD (the σmin\sigma_{\min} direction) as its probe direction uu, so the incremental cost is one forward+backward (0.420.42 ms) but the assembled cost is σmin\sigma_{\min} + probe (38.538.5 ms). The λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) and LLC observables are independent pipelines that do not consume prior outputs. The LLC row is included as a cost reference for readers who use it as their default complexity invariant.

Scale-dependence of the cost ordering. At Barak’s h=500h{=}500, N=2,048N{=}2{,}048 regime, the fp64 activation SVD (∼h2​N\sim h^{2}N) and the fp64 Fisher eigh (∼h3\sim h^{3}) land in comparable wall-clock, so λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) at 1616 ms happens to be cheaper than σmin\sigma_{\min} at 3838 ms. This ordering is scale-dependent: at LLM widths (h∼104h\sim 10^{4}, N≳104N\gtrsim 10^{4}) the Fisher eigh cost scales cubically in hh while the SVD and FBP costs scale linearly in hh, so λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) becomes the bottleneck and the FBP ordering (σmin\sigma_{\min} cheapest, u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu near-free given σmin\sigma_{\min}, λmin​(G)\lambda_{\min}(G) expensive) reasserts itself. The body’s cost-ordering paragraph (§4) makes this scale split explicit.

B.8.2 Bridge structural prediction: multi-seed trajectory correlation

The per-Aoyagi-cell structural correlation in §4.4 validates the framework’s prediction λmin+​(Gℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ)2\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2} at the cross-cell level on closed-form RLCT testbeds. As an independent confirmation that the same structural prediction holds as a joint trajectory scaling on a real-network testbed (not only as a cross-cell ranking on parametric singular families), we run the per-checkpoint observable suite of §B.8 at extended length on Barak SGD++MSE and report the Spearman rank correlation between σmin​(Xh1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}}) and the smallest positive eigenvalue λmin+​(Gh1)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{1}}) across the post-grok descent.

Random-direction null discrimination.

A natural reviewer concern is that udeadu_{\mathrm{dead}} in the bolded reading above is the bottom right-singular vector of Xh1X_{h_{1}}, then re-projected into u⊤​Gh1​uu^{\top}G_{h_{1}}u on the same trajectory, so the structural correlation could be partly an SVD-basis artefact rather than genuine geometric signal. We adversarially test this by extending the per-checkpoint probe to four directions in addition to udeadu_{\mathrm{dead}}: urand∼Unif⁡(Sd−1)u_{\mathrm{rand}}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(S^{d-1}) (full random-direction null), ubot​-​K⟂u_{\mathrm{bot}\text{-}K\,\perp} uniform on the bottom-1010 singular subspace of Xh1X_{h_{1}} orthogonal to udeadu_{\mathrm{dead}} (partial shared rank-deficiency control), and utopu_{\mathrm{top}} the top right-singular vector of Xh1X_{h_{1}}. Each direction is fixed once per checkpoint (seeded; logged in metadata) and the same Phase A Spearman ρ\rho vs σmin​(Xh1)\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}}) is computed for each. On Barak SGD++MSE the random-direction null is decisively rejected: ρ⁡(udead)=+0.875±0.148\rho(u_{\mathrm{dead}})=+0.875\pm 0.148 (reproducing the bolded row above to within seed dispersion) vs ρ⁡(urand)=+0.048±0.157\rho(u_{\mathrm{rand}})=+0.048\pm 0.157 (indistinguishable from zero), Δ​ρ=+0.83\Delta\rho=+0.83. On the Nanda AdamW++CE testbed, where trajectory rate-fits are disclaimed (Remark 80), the same protocol gives ρ⁡(udead)=+0.794±0.086\rho(u_{\mathrm{dead}})=+0.794\pm 0.086 vs ρ⁡(urand)=+0.438±0.194\rho(u_{\mathrm{rand}})=+0.438\pm 0.194, Δ​ρ=+0.36\Delta\rho=+0.36, the dead direction still carries 1.8×1.8\times the random-direction signal, with the residual non-zero ρ⁡(urand)\rho(u_{\mathrm{rand}}) reflecting weaker but non-zero coupling between random hidden directions and σmin\sigma_{\min} in this regime. The expected ordering ρ⁡(udead)>ρ⁡(ubot​-​K⟂)>ρ⁡(utop)≳ρ⁡(urand)\rho(u_{\mathrm{dead}})>\rho(u_{\mathrm{bot}\text{-}K\,\perp})>\rho(u_{\mathrm{top}})\gtrsim\rho(u_{\mathrm{rand}}) holds on both testbeds (Figure 10), with ubot​-​K⟂u_{\mathrm{bot}\text{-}K\,\perp} carrying the partial shared-rank-deficiency signal and utopu_{\mathrm{top}} closer to the random null. The structural correlation reading is therefore a property of the dead direction specifically, not a measurement artefact of the SVD-basis choice.

Canonical-bridge cross-validation.

For an analytical-limit reference point on the same correlation, we run the same trajectory protocol on a canonical-bridge testbed (square L=2L=2 linear, diagonal canonical init, full-batch deterministic gradient flow; see Shirodkar 2026for the parametric anchor) for 55 seeds ×\times 20,00020{,}000 steps (402 ckpts/seed at fp64). The Spearman correlation between σmin​(Xh)\sigma_{\min}(X_{h}) and λmin+​(Gh)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h}) is +1.000000±0.000000\mathbf{+1.000000\pm 0.000000} across all 5/55/5 seeds, with log-log slope 2.193±0.0232.193\pm 0.023 over ∼1.1\sim 1.1 OOM in σmin\sigma_{\min}. The end-to-end picture: the predicted structural correlation holds at ρ→1\rho\to 1 deterministically in the analytical limit, and at ρ=+0.83±0.13\rho=+0.83\pm 0.13 across 3030 noisy SGD seeds on Barak.

Phase A vs Phase B contrast.

The dead-direction cluster does not cohere in Phase B (post-σmin\sigma_{\min} minimum). Phase B per-pair correlations drop to |ρ|≤0.31|\rho|\leq 0.31 for the bridge-prediction pair λmin+​(Gh1)↔σmin​(Xh1)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{1}})\leftrightarrow\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}}) (ρB=+0.228±0.120\rho_{B}=+0.228\pm 0.120 across 44 seeds with ≥6\geq 6 Phase B checkpoints) and ρB=+0.306±0.187\rho_{B}=+0.306\pm 0.187 for u⊤​G​u↔σminu^{\top}Gu\leftrightarrow\sigma_{\min}. This is by construction: in the post-σmin\sigma_{\min}-minimum NESS the trajectory is no longer monotonically descending in σmin\sigma_{\min}; it oscillates within the gauge orbit, so cross-trajectory correlation between observables that the framework predicts to scale as powers of tt is no longer well-defined. Function-space and live-direction observables (val_acc, σmax​(Xh1)\sigma_{\max}(X_{h_{1}}), LLC, eff​_​rank​(Xh1)\mathrm{eff\_rank}(X_{h_{1}})) drift ≤5%\leq 5\% across Phase B in the same window where σmin\sigma_{\min} drifts an order of magnitude, the post-Phase-A regime is function-preserving gauge-orbit oscillation.

Methodology note.

The Phase A slope-fit reading and the Phase A correlation reading ρ=+0.832±0.126\rho=+0.832\pm 0.126 here are different summaries of the same underlying scaling, computed from the same canonical 3030-seed Barak run (240240k SGD steps, fp64): the slope-fit reads the asymptotic exponent from a log-log fit and is sensitive to whether σmin\sigma_{\min} at the start of the post-grok descent sits above the floating-point floor with enough headroom to develop a measurable Phase A; the rank correlation reads the joint co-monotonicity of two observables along the trajectory at any monotonic transformation and is robust to that precondition. At canonical n/D=33n/D{=}33, four of five seeds satisfy the descent precondition and read slope ≈2\approx 2 (x¯=2.06±0.20\bar{x}=2.06\pm 0.20); at n/D∈{167,833}n/D\in\{167,833\} the geometric event compresses below practical save cadence and the slope fit is not interpretable as the framework’s predicted exponent. The structural rank-level prediction λmin+​(G)∝σmin​(X)2\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G)\propto\sigma_{\min}(X)^{2} holds across all 3030 canonical seeds; the quantitative slope-22 prediction is in scope where the descent is resolvable.

Theory anchor for the observable suite.

Every parameter-space and Fisher-side observable in our suite is the empirical signature of a specific result in the rate chain (Table 4). Activation-side observables (σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}), σ(r0)​(Xℓ)\sigma_{(r_{0})}(X_{\ell}), r0r_{0}, eff_rank) anchor on Corollary 58 and the selection rule (Theorem 3). Fisher-side observables (λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), λmax​(G)\lambda_{\max}(G), u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu at probe directions) anchor on Thm. 21. Curvature and volume proxies (κ\kappa, logdet+\log\det^{+}) anchor on the Fisher–curvature–volume rate chain (Proposition 8). Hessian observables (trace, sharpness) are reported as standard reference points, related to the Fisher via Gauss–Newton at well-converged minima but not directly predicted by the rate chain. LLC [Lau et al. 2025, Hoogland et al. 2024] is included as the singular-learning-theory comparison baseline; it is not derived from the rate-chain framework.

Volume-side proxy and full multi-layer rate chain on a noisy NN.

The volume side of the rate chain (Corollary 8) predicts logdet+(Gℓ)∝klogσmin\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto k\log\sigma_{\min} on the active subspace, where det+\det^{+} denotes the product of strictly-positive eigenvalues. Unlike the bridge structural and curvature-side predictions which are about a single eigenvalue, logdet+\log\det^{+} is a full-spectrum observable and requires both (i) sufficient n/dn/d to resolve the entire spectrum stably and (ii) a trajectory descending into a singular minimum. On the canonical bridge (L=2L=2 linear, D=6D=6, n/d=333n/d{=}333, deterministic descent), the prediction validates cleanly at ρ(logdet+,logσmin)=+1.000000±0\rho(\log\det^{+},\log\sigma_{\min})=+1.000000\pm 0 across 5/55/5 seeds.

To extend the test to a noisy NN trajectory satisfying both preconditions, we run an L=4L{=}4 deep-linear noisy bridge: y=W4​W3​W2​W1​xy=W_{4}W_{3}W_{2}W_{1}x with diagonal canonical init Wℓ=diag⁡(1,…,1,t0)W_{\ell}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,1,t_{0}) for every ℓ\ell, target y=M⋆​x+εy=M^{\star}x+\varepsilon with M⋆=diag⁡(1,…,1,0)M^{\star}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0) (rank-11 deficit), D=20D{=}20, N=2000N{=}2000 (n/d=100n/d{=}100), σ=0.1\sigma{=}0.1. The framework predicts per-layer rates: with σmin​(Xℓ)∝|t|ℓ\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})\propto|t|^{\ell} along the canonical descent and λmin+​(Gℓ)∝t2​(L−ℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto t^{2(L-\ell)}, the slope ∂log⁡(rateobservable)/∂log⁡σmin​(Xℓ)\partial\log\mathrm{(rateobservable)}/\partial\log\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) equals 2​(L−ℓ)/ℓ2(L-\ell)/\ell at each layer. The same 2​(L−ℓ)/ℓ2(L-\ell)/\ell structure governs logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) and −κ⁡(Gℓ)-\kappa(G_{\ell}). Observed slopes deviate from the leading-order predictions by a positive offset that grows from ∼13%\sim 13\% at ℓ=1\ell{=}1 to ∼40%\sim 40\% at ℓ=3\ell{=}3: the expected finite-tt Taylor correction for the canonical-aligned trajectory at t0=0.5t_{0}{=}0.5 (offsets shrink to ≤1%\leq 1\% at t≤0.3t\leq 0.3). The offset is intrinsic to finite-tt slope-fits, not a measurement noise issue; rank correlations ρ=+1\rho{=}+1 across all cells confirm the predicted joint scaling without depending on slope magnitudes, and the slope ratio between r=2r{=}2 and r=1r{=}1 (next paragraph) cancels the offset and lands within 1.5%1.5\% of the predicted exact factor of 22. Under squared-error loss the residual prefactor of the loss-gradient covariance (Remark 4) is a second contribution to the per-layer slope offset alongside the finite-tt Taylor correction; it enters every layer’s logdet+\log\det^{+} as a common factor and so cancels in the rank-multiplicative r=2r{=}2/r=1r{=}1 ratio, which is why the discriminating test (next paragraph) recovers the exact factor of 22 while the absolute per-layer slopes carry the offset.

Multi-direction extension (rank-2 deficit).

A direct test of Proposition 8’s multi-direction generalisation comes from running the same bridge with rank-deficit r=2r{=}2 (two dead directions): M⋆=diag⁡(1,…,1,0,0)M^{\star}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,0) and Wℓ=diag⁡(1,…,1,t0,t0)W_{\ell}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,1,t_{0},t_{0}) for every ℓ\ell. The framework predicts that the rr dead directions contribute additively to the log-determinant: logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope scales as r⋅2​(L−ℓ)/ℓr\cdot 2(L-\ell)/\ell, while λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}) slope is independent of rr (only the smallest dead eigenvalue matters; both dead eigenvalues are equal under the symmetric init). Rank-multiplicative identity: 77-cell robustness sweep.

The identity test has a measurable precondition, and this cell locates its boundary.

Higher rank-deficit (r=3,4r{=}3,4).

The factor-of-22 at r=2r{=}2 is the smallest case of a linear law in rr. Running each of the 77 configurations at rank-deficit r=3r{=}3 and r=4r{=}4 (the last rr entries of M⋆M^{\star} set to zero) extends the test along its discriminating axis. Pooled across the configurations, seeds, and layers, the logdet+\log\det^{+} slope ratio against the rank-11 baseline reads 1.96±0.091.96\pm 0.09, 3.13±0.513.13\pm 0.51, 3.97±0.653.97\pm 0.65 at r=2,3,4r{=}2,3,4 against the predicted 2,3,42,3,4, while the matching λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+} slope stays rank-invariant (the rate chain holds at ρ=0.985\rho{=}0.985 mean across the sweep; Fig. 4). The cell-to-cell spread widens with rr (the higher-rank descents leave less of the spectrum above the noise floor under a fixed step budget), but every rank sits on the y=ry{=}r line: the volume slope counts the dead directions, and the count is the rank-deficit.

The verified domain of the volume-side rate chain therefore includes the analytic limit (L=2L{=}2 canonical bridge), and a multi-cell noisy multi-layer NN sweep at L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\}, D∈{20,50}D\in\{20,50\}, full and mini-batch SGD, rank-deficit r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\}, with the asymptotic-regime precondition empirically characterised at t0L≳σnoise2t_{0}^{L}\gtrsim\sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}^{2}.

Comprehensive observable map.

The same L=4L{=}4 noisy-bridge experiment confirms the framework’s predictions across the entire 11-observable suite tracked by the per-layer probe (Table 5). The framework partitions observables into two classes: those that should descend with the dead-direction trajectory (rate-chain primaries plus their rank-aware companions) and those that should stay bounded (live-direction probes and rank-invariant diagnostics). Both classes are confirmed simultaneously: dead-direction observables track σmin\sigma_{\min} at ρ=±1.000\rho{=}{\pm}1.000 with the predicted layer-graded slopes, while live-direction observables show ρ≈0\rho{\approx}0 and constant-or-near-constant magnitudes throughout the trajectory. The basis-stability cosine empirically confirms that canonical alignment is preserved under SGD on this trajectory, a precondition for the rate-chain predictions that the framework requires but typically takes as an assumption.

Cross-testbed universality of the structural correlation.

The dead-direction correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(Gh1),σmin​(Xh1))\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{h_{1}}),\,\sigma_{\min}(X_{h_{1}})) holds robustly across four testbeds spanning architecture, optimizer, loss, training-task complexity, and dynamic range:

Barak sparse parity (MLP, Phase A) SGD+mom + MSE yes ∼10\sim\!10 OOM +0.832±0.126\mathbf{+0.832\pm 0.126}
Nanda mod. add (1-blk transformer, no grok) SGD+mom + MSE no ∼28\sim\!28 OOM +0.846±0.014\mathbf{+0.846\pm 0.014}

Seed counts: canonical bridge 1010 seeds, Barak 3030 seeds, Nanda SGD++MSE 1010 seeds, Nanda AdamW++CE 1010 seeds; per-pair ρ\rho’s are computed across the trajectory (≥50\geq 50 checkpoints/seed). On Barak the 55-seed Phase-A subset gives +0.872±0.060+0.872\pm 0.060 and the full 3030-seed run +0.832±0.126+0.832\pm 0.126; the dispersion widens with the larger sample. The structural correlation ≥+0.75\geq+0.75 across testbeds spanning ∼1\sim 1 to ∼28\sim 28 orders of magnitude in σmin\sigma_{\min} dynamic range, both grokking and non-grokking trajectories, both SGD- and Adam-class optimizers, both MSE and CE losses, both MLP and transformer architectures. The Nanda AdamW+CE row is the strongest universality test: trajectory rate-fits (slope-fitting on u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu) fail in the AdamW+CE regime (the canonical-alignment hypothesis is violated; see body §4.4), but the structural correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min}) does not require the trajectory to be canonical-aligned, it only requires both observables to be reading the same underlying rank-deficient geometry, which they do independently of how the trajectory navigates that geometry. It is the lowest of the four testbeds, where the rate-fit precondition fails most cleanly, but the cross-seed mean stays well above zero. The Nanda SGD+MSE-without-grok row demonstrates the same point in the opposite extreme: the trajectory descends 2828 OOM in σmin\sigma_{\min} in a degenerate-collapse regime where the network never learns the task, and the structural correlation is much tighter (ρ=+0.846\rho=+0.846, std =0.014=0.014). Joint with the within-trajectory consistency check ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),u⊤​G​u)=+0.81\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),u^{\top}Gu)=+0.81 (Barak) and +0.92+0.92 (Nanda Adam+CE), the multi-testbed picture is that λmin+​(Gℓ)∝σmin​(Xℓ)2\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell})\propto\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell})^{2} is a geometric property of the bridge stratum, not a property of any specific descent dynamics on it. The structural correlation is a Spearman rank statistic, so it is invariant to any monotone reweighting of λmin+​(G)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G), including the global residual prefactor that distinguishes the stored loss-gradient covariance from the population Fisher (Remark 4). The estimator question that scopes the slope-fit therefore leaves the structural reading untouched: a prefactor that shifts a fitted exponent cannot move a co-monotonicity ranking. The Nanda AdamW+CE cell uses the true-MC Fisher (labels sampled from the model softmax), the principled estimand for a CE task where the empirical true-label Fisher collapses as the loss approaches zero; switching from the empirical Fisher to true-MC shifts ρ\rho from +0.774+0.774 to +0.751+0.751, a −0.023-0.023 change well within the cross-seed std, empirically confirming the rank statistic’s robustness to the Fisher estimand.

B.9 Compute and reproducibility

All experiments run on a single workstation: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9955WX (16c/32t), 256 GB DDR5 ECC, 4×4\times NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB). Total compute to reproduce the experiments reported in this paper: ∼\sim3535 GPU-hours, dominated by the 3030-seed grokking observable hierarchy on Nanda modular addition and Barak sparse parity (240240k steps each at fp6464).

The experiments reported in the body and bound appendix are: Aoyagi closed-form RLCT validation on the rectangular RRR anchor (1414 cells ×\times 55 seeds ×\times 33 noise levels) and the square DLN-RRR sweep (2424 cells ×\times 55 seeds), with the DLN-RRR LLC three-calibration audit on the same cells (App. B.6, App. B.5); the Nanda transformer width sweep (44 widths ×\times 3030 seeds AdamW++CE) plus 9×9\times LLC budget confirmation at dmodel=128d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}128 (§4.3); the grokking observable hierarchy (Nanda mod-add and Barak sparse parity, 3030 seeds each, 5050k / 240240k steps respectively; App. B.8); the Barak n/Dn/D sweep at ntrain∈{5000,25000}n_{\mathrm{train}}\in\{5000,25000\} with the cadence-bounded fine-resolution probe; the TMS sparsity sweep (66 sparsities ×\times 55 seeds at two configurations; App. B.7); and the rank-multiplicative noisy-bridge sweep across 77 cells (L∈{4,6,8}L\in\{4,6,8\}, D∈{20,50}D\in\{20,50\}, full and mini-batch SGD, 55 seeds per cell at r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\}; App. B.8.2).

Per-experiment wall-clock and GPU usage is recorded in each result JSON’s metadata block (run_started_at, gpu_model, cuda_visible_devices); aggregate per-sweep timing is reproducible from the launcher logs under the corresponding results/ directory. The parametric and ablation experiments referenced by Shirodkar 2026 (two-layer autoencoder rate-fits, preconditioner-knob ablations, compatibility-boundary sweep) are reproduced in the theory paper.

Code release.

The experiment scripts, the σmin\sigma_{\min} core library, KFAC implementation, calibration tooling, result JSONs, and figure-generation scripts will be released publicly on GitHub under an open-source license; in the interim they are available from the authors on request.

Per-experiment seed lists and exact hyperparameters are documented in each script’s header.

Reproducibility audit.

Every numerical claim in the paper is anchored to a specific JSON via a provenance comment in the originating chunk. A canonical audit script (included in the code release) verifies in one command that every cited path resolves on disk, every figure target is present, and headline numbers (Aoyagi anchor cross-cell ρ\rho and the noise-robustness sweep, the Aoyagi 2024 DLN cells, the Nanda transformer width-sweep ρ\rho values + 9×9\times-budget split, the Barak Phase A structural correlation, the multi-direction ratio test across r∈{1,2,3,4}r\in\{1,2,3,4\}) reproduce within tolerance from their cited JSONs. The script runs as a pre-build gate before paper compilation; bootstrap CIs are used on the heavy-tailed Barak readings rather than parametric ±1.96​σ\pm 1.96\sigma.

Appendix C Optimiser ×\times loss applicability of the empirical observables

We do not introduce new observables in this paper; we use existing observables from the singular-learning, KFAC, and spectral-monitoring literatures. The formal applicability conditions for the rate predictions are stated in Shirodkar 2026. This appendix is a defensive scope reference: it classifies each observable used in this paper by the optimiser ×\times loss combinations under which it remains a valid signal versus those under which its signal is dominated by the Adam non-equivariance failure mode (Remark 80). The matrix is the easiest reference for “why does the structural correlation hold under AdamW++CE when the trajectory rate-fits do not.”

C.1 Static vs trajectory observable applicability

The framework has two distinct classes of observables, validated under different conditions. Mixing them up is the most common reproducer failure mode.

Static observables

(well-defined at any single checkpoint, no trajectory required):

  • •

    σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) at any layer

  • •

    σmax​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\max}(X_{\ell}), effective rank, full activation SVD

  • •

    u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu at a fixed direction uu (single backward pass), reading Fisher magnitude but not a rate

  • •

    Expected-Fisher spectrum at a single checkpoint

These are valid for any optimizer, any loss, any architecture. Every DDS observable in this paper sits in this class: σmin​(Xℓ)\sigma_{\min}(X_{\ell}) at the dimension-fixed boundary layer of the Aoyagi anchor (§B.6) and on the Nanda transformer width sweep (§4.3), and λmin+​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\ell}), logdet+(Gℓ)\log\det^{+}(G_{\ell}) read at the converged checkpoint.

Trajectory-rate observables

(require an actual approach to a singular minimum; rate has meaning only along the trajectory):

  • •

    Power-law slope of u⊤​G​uu^{\top}Gu vs tt (or vs σmin\sigma_{\min}, the scale-free ratio)

  • •

    Power-law slope of λmin​(Gℓ)\lambda_{\min}(G_{\ell}) or λp−1​(Fhpop)\lambda_{p-1}(F_{h}^{\mathrm{pop}}) along training

  • •

    Per-layer rate exponent matching Theorem 21’s 2​(L−ℓ)2(L-\ell) prediction

These are valid only when (a) the optimizer is theorem-compatible (SGD on GG-invariant metrics, or empirically Shampoo full-batch and KFAC++KL-clip full-batch on canonical-bridge testbeds), AND (b) the trajectory actually approaches a singular minimum AND (c) the trajectory is canonical-aligned (gauge-redundant losses ++ noise-amplifying preconditioners fail (b); random init typically violates (c)). Outside this regime, trajectory rate-fits are unsupported, but the structural correlation ρ⁡(λmin+​(G),σmin)\rho(\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G),\sigma_{\min}) remains a geometric property and is empirically validated multi-seed including under AdamW++CE on a Nanda transformer (§B.8.2).
